m3-l001-linear-combinations-span-dot-pro.prompt: The vectors $v_1=(1,0,2)$, $v_2=(0,1,1)$, $v_3=(1,1,3)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are given. What is their span?
options: All of $\mathbb{R}^3$, because three vectors always span three-dimensional space.
A line through the origin, because all three vectors have positive entries.
A plane that misses the origin.
A plane through the origin, because $v_3=v_1+v_2$ adds nothing new.
m3-l001-linear-combinations-span-dot-pro.explanation: Since $v_3 = v_1 + v_2$, the third vector is already in the span of the first two. Counting vectors does not give the dimension; only independent directions count. A span always contains the zero vector.

m3-l001-linear-combinations-span-dot-pro.prompt: Find the angle in degrees between $u=(1,2,2)$ and $v=(3,0,4)$. Give the answer in degrees.
m3-l001-linear-combinations-span-dot-pro.explanation: $\cos\theta = \dfrac{u\cdot v}{|u||v|} = \dfrac{11}{3\cdot 5}=\dfrac{11}{15}$, so $\theta \approx 42.8^\circ$. Cauchy-Schwarz guarantees this ratio is between $-1$ and $1$.

m3-l001-linear-combinations-span-dot-pro.prompt: In your own words, what is the span of a set of vectors, and why does the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $|v\cdot w|\le\|v\|\|w\|$ hold? Use the angle between $v$ and $w$.
m3-l001-linear-combinations-span-dot-pro.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the span is the set of all linear combinations $c_1v_1+\dots+c_kv_k$ (a line, plane, or all of the space, always through the origin); (2) $v\cdot w=\|v\|\|w\|\cos\theta$; (3) since $|\cos\theta|\le1$, the dot product cannot exceed the product of the lengths, with equality only when the vectors are parallel.
m3-l001-linear-combinations-span-dot-pro.modelAnswer: The span of $v_1,\dots,v_k$ is every linear combination $c_1v_1+\dots+c_kv_k$: a line, a plane, or more, but always passing through the origin. Because $v\cdot w=\|v\|\|w\|\cos\theta$ and $|\cos\theta|\le1$, we get $|v\cdot w|\le\|v\|\|w\|$, with equality exactly when $v$ and $w$ are parallel.

m3-l002-matrix-times-vector-column-pictu.prompt: For a matrix $A$ and vector $x$, which statement about $Ax=b$ is correct?
options: Solvable exactly when $b$ is in the span of the rows of $A$.
Solvable exactly when $b$ is in the span of the columns of $A$.
Solvable exactly when $b$ is perpendicular to every column of $A$.
Solvable whenever $A$ has at least as many rows as columns.
m3-l002-matrix-times-vector-column-pictu.explanation: $Ax = x_1\,\text{col}_1 + \dots + x_n\,\text{col}_n$, so $Ax=b$ asks whether $b$ is a linear combination of the columns, and $x$ lists the coefficients. Row spans and shapes alone do not decide solvability.

m3-l002-matrix-times-vector-column-pictu.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\\0&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=(3,-1)$. Compute $Ax$ as $3\,\text{col}_1 - 1\,\text{col}_2$ and give its third component.
m3-l002-matrix-times-vector-column-pictu.explanation: $Ax = 3(2,1,0) - (1,3,4) = (5,0,-4)$. The third component is $-4$: the column view builds $Ax$ one column at a time.
equations: A x = x_1 a_1 + x_2 a_2 + \dots + x_n a_n

m3-l002-matrix-times-vector-column-pictu.prompt: In your own words, explain why viewing $Ax$ as a combination of the columns of $A$ is the picture that generalises, and what question $Ax=b$ is asking in that picture.
m3-l002-matrix-times-vector-column-pictu.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $Ax$ is a sum of columns weighted by the entries of $x$; (2) the set of all $Ax$ is the span of the columns (the column space), so $Ax=b$ asks whether $b$ is in that span; (3) a reason it generalises (works for any shape, leads to subspaces and rank, whereas row dot products are just one way to compute entries).
m3-l002-matrix-times-vector-column-pictu.modelAnswer: Each entry of $x$ is the amount of one column of $A$ you mix in, so $Ax$ is a recipe for building a vector from the columns. Every possible output is therefore a point in the span of the columns, and $Ax=b$ asks whether the target $b$ can be built from those ingredients. This view carries over to any matrix shape and leads straight to column space, rank and basis, while the row-by-row dot-product view only tells you how to compute one number at a time.

m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.prompt: The system $2x+y=5$, $x-y=1$ is drawn in both pictures. What does the column picture show?
options: Two lines in the plane that meet at the single point $(2,1)$.
The columns $(2,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ are perpendicular, so no solution exists.
The vector $(5,1)$ equals $2(2,1)+1(1,-1)$, a combination of the columns.
The vector $(5,1)$ lies along the first column $(2,1)$, so $y=0$.
m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.explanation: Solving gives $x=2$, $y=1$, and $2(2,1)+1(1,-1)=(5,1)$: the right-hand side is built from the columns. The first option is the row picture, where the solution is where two lines cross.

m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.prompt: Eliminate on $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&-6&0\\-2&7&2\end{pmatrix}$ (no row exchanges). What is the third pivot?
m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.explanation: Subtract 2 times row 1 from row 2 (multiplier 2) and $-1$ times row 1 from row 3. Then row 3 minus $(-1)$ times row 2 gives the pivot $1$. The pivots are $2,-8,1$.

m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.prompt: For the same matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&-6&0\\-2&7&2\end{pmatrix}$, what is the multiplier $\ell_{32}$ used to clear the $(3,2)$ position after the first column is cleared?
m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.explanation: After step one, rows 2 and 3 are $(0,-8,-2)$ and $(0,8,3)$, so $\ell_{32} = 8/(-8) = -1$. Each multiplier becomes an entry of $E_{32}$ (and later of $L$).

m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.prompt: During elimination, what is a pivot, what does a multiplier $\ell_{ij}$ record, and what does it tell you if a pivot position turns out to be zero with no row below it that can fix it?
m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a pivot is the entry used to clear the entries below it in its column; (2) the multiplier $\ell_{ij}=a_{ij}/a_{jj}$ is how many copies of the pivot row are subtracted from row $i$; (3) if a pivot cannot be found in some column, the system is singular: it has either no solution or infinitely many.
m3-l003-row-column-pictures-gaussian-eli.modelAnswer: The pivot is the entry in the current row and column that is used to eliminate the entries below it. The multiplier $\ell_{ij}=a_{ij}/a_{jj}$ records how many copies of the pivot row are subtracted from row $i$. If a column has no usable pivot (even after row exchanges), the matrix is singular, and the system has either no solution or infinitely many.

m3-l004-elimination-outcomes-elementary-.prompt: The system $x+y=2$, $2x+2y=5$ is solved by elimination. What happens and what does it mean?
options: Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives $0=1$, so the system is inconsistent and has no solution.
Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives $0=0$, so there are infinitely many solutions.
Elimination produces two pivots, so the solution is unique and easy to find.
A solution must exist, because there are as many equations as unknowns here.
m3-l004-elimination-outcomes-elementary-.explanation: Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 gives $0x+0y = 1$. A missing pivot with an inconsistent right-hand side means the two lines are parallel and never meet. Square shape does not guarantee a solution; the pivots decide.

m3-l004-elimination-outcomes-elementary-.prompt: After elimination on a $3\times3$ system you reach a final row $(0\;0\;0\,|\,0)$ and only two pivots. What does the row picture show?
options: Three planes meet at exactly one point.
The three planes have no common point, because a row of zeros appeared.
Three planes share a whole line of solutions, with one free variable.
Two planes are identical and the third is parallel to them, so no solution exists.
m3-l004-elimination-outcomes-elementary-.explanation: The last equation reads $0=0$, so it is consistent but carries no information: one free variable remains and the planes share a line. A contradictory row like $(0\;0\;0\,|\,1)$ would instead mean no solution.

m3-l004-elimination-outcomes-elementary-.prompt: Explain how a $2\times 2$ system looks in the row picture and in the column picture, and how elimination (done as multiplication by elementary matrices $E_{ij}$) tells you which of the three outcomes occurs.
m3-l004-elimination-outcomes-elementary-.rubric: Full credit requires: row picture = two lines meeting (or not); column picture = combining column vectors to reach the right-hand side; elimination step = left-multiplication by $E_{ij}$ with the multiplier; pivots decide outcome: full pivots -> unique, missing pivot with inconsistent row -> none, missing pivot with consistent row -> infinitely many.
m3-l004-elimination-outcomes-elementary-.modelAnswer: In the row picture each equation is a line and the solution is where they cross; in the column picture the two columns are vectors and we ask what mix of them reaches the right side. Each elimination step subtracts a multiple of one row from another, which is multiplication by an elementary matrix $E_{ij}$ holding that multiplier. If we get a full set of pivots the solution is unique; if a pivot is missing we either hit a contradiction like $0=1$ (no solution, parallel lines) or $0=0$ (a free variable, infinitely many solutions).

m3-l005-matrix-multiplication-four-views.prompt: Rotate a book $90^\circ$ about the $x$-axis and then $90^\circ$ about the $y$-axis. Doing the two rotations in the opposite order gives a different final orientation. What does this show?
options: Matrix multiplication is not associative, which is why the order of rotations matters.
Finite rotations commute, so the different results must come from sloppy rotating.
Rotation matrices do not commute, so $AB\ne BA$, although multiplication is associative.
The final orientations agree, because both orders rotate through the same total angle.
m3-l005-matrix-multiplication-four-views.explanation: Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative, and 3D rotations are the standard physical example. This non-commutativity underlies angular-momentum commutators later on.

m3-l005-matrix-multiplication-four-views.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(2,2)$ entry of $AB$.
m3-l005-matrix-multiplication-four-views.explanation: Row 2 of $A$ times column 2 of $B$: $3\cdot1 + 4\cdot2 = 11$. Equivalently $AB=\sum_k(\text{col}_k A)(\text{row}_k B)$, whose $(2,2)$ entry is $3\cdot1+4\cdot2$.

m3-l005-matrix-multiplication-four-views.prompt: Describe two different ways to compute a product $AB$ and say what each is good for. Why is $AB\ne BA$ in general although $(AB)C=A(BC)$?
m3-l005-matrix-multiplication-four-views.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) any two views: row times column gives each entry as a dot product; columns of $A$ combined by the entries of each column of $B$; rows of $B$ combined by the rows of $A$; or columns times rows summing to rank-one pieces; (2) $AB$ means 'apply $B$ first, then $A$', and doing two operations in a different order generally gives a different result (e.g. rotations); (3) associativity holds because grouping does not change the order in which the operations are applied.
m3-l005-matrix-multiplication-four-views.modelAnswer: Each entry $(AB)_{ij}$ is row $i$ of $A$ dotted with column $j$ of $B$; equivalently each column of $AB$ is $A$ times a column of $B$, i.e. a combination of the columns of $A$. The first view is best for computing a single entry, the second for understanding what $AB$ does to vectors. $AB$ means 'do $B$, then $A$', so reversing the order generally changes the outcome (rotations about different axes do not commute), but regrouping a chain without changing its order, $(AB)C=A(BC)$, cannot matter.

m3-l006-inverses-gauss-jordan.prompt: If $A$ and $B$ are invertible, which expression equals $(AB)^{-1}$?
options: $B^{-1}A^{-1}$, since the last operation applied must be undone first.
$A^{-1}B^{-1}$, since inverses can be applied in whichever order is convenient.
$A^{-1}+B^{-1}$, since the inverse of a product splits into a sum of inverses.
$(A+B)^{-1}$, since the inverse of a product equals the inverse of the sum.
m3-l006-inverses-gauss-jordan.explanation: $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1}) = A(BB^{-1})A^{-1} = I$. The order reverses because the last operation applied must be the first one undone.

m3-l006-inverses-gauss-jordan.prompt: Using Gauss-Jordan elimination (or the $2\times2$ formula), find the $(2,1)$ entry of $A^{-1}$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\7&6\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l006-inverses-gauss-jordan.explanation: $\det A = 24-14 = 10$ and $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{10}\begin{pmatrix}6&-2\\-7&4\end{pmatrix}$, so the $(2,1)$ entry is $-0.7$.

m3-l006-inverses-gauss-jordan.prompt: Why does the order reverse in $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$, and how can you tell from the pivots (Gauss-Jordan) whether a square matrix has an inverse?
m3-l006-inverses-gauss-jordan.rubric: Full credit requires: an everyday or algebraic argument for reversal (undo the last step first; verify $(AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=I$); and that an inverse exists iff elimination produces $n$ pivots (Gauss-Jordan turns $[A\,|\,I]$ into $[I\,|\,A^{-1}]$), failing when a pivot is missing.
m3-l006-inverses-gauss-jordan.modelAnswer: If $AB$ means 'do $B$, then $A$', undoing it requires first undoing $A$ and then undoing $B$, giving $B^{-1}A^{-1}$ (put on socks, then shoes; remove shoes first). Algebraically $AB\,B^{-1}A^{-1}=A\,I\,A^{-1}=I$. For existence, run Gauss-Jordan on $[A\,|\,I]$: if you get $n$ pivots you can reduce the left block to $I$ and the right block is $A^{-1}$; a missing pivot means the matrix is singular and has no inverse.

m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.prompt: In $A=LU$ (no row exchanges), why can the multipliers be written into $L$ exactly as they were used, with no mixing?
options: $L$ is the product of the elimination matrices $E_{ij}$ themselves, in the order applied.
The multipliers are stored in $U$, and $L$ is simply the identity matrix here.
$L$ holds the pivots, which never change during elimination, so no mixing arises.
$L$ is built from the inverse steps in reverse order, which do not interact.
m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.explanation: $E_{32}E_{31}E_{21}A=U$ gives $A=E_{21}^{-1}E_{31}^{-1}E_{32}^{-1}U$. Each inverse just flips the sign of its multiplier, and in this order the multipliers drop into $L$ directly. The product of the $E$ themselves would mix them.

m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.prompt: You must solve $Ax=b$ for 1000 different right-hand sides with the same large $A$. What is the efficient strategy?
options: Run full Gaussian elimination again for each new $b$, since the multipliers depend on $b$.
Factor $A=LU$ once (about $n^3/3$ operations), then do a forward and a back substitution per $b$ (about $n^2$).
Refactor $A$ for every $b$, because $L$ and $U$ change when the right-hand side changes.
Compute $A^{-1}$ from scratch for every $b$, since only an inverse can be reused.
m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.explanation: The factorisation depends only on $A$, not on $b$. After the one-time $n^3/3$ cost, each solve costs about $n^2$ for the two triangular solves.

m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.prompt: Use $A=LU$ to solve $Ax=b$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&-6&0\\-2&7&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=(5,-2,9)$. Give $x_3$.
m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.explanation: Forward substitution $Lc=b$ gives $c=(5,-12,2)$, then back substitution $Ux=c$ gives $x=(1,1,2)$, so $x_3=2$.

m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.prompt: Explain what $L$ and $U$ each store after elimination, and why factoring $A=LU$ once is the efficient way to solve $Ax=b$ for many different right-hand sides $b$.
m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $U$ is the upper-triangular result of elimination and $L$ is lower-triangular with the multipliers $\ell_{ij}$ (and ones on its diagonal); (2) solving $Lc=b$ by forward substitution and $Ux=c$ by back substitution costs only about $n^2$ operations; (3) the expensive step (about $n^3/3$ operations) depends only on $A$, so it is done once and reused for every $b$.
m3-l007-lu-factorisation-substitution.modelAnswer: $U$ is the triangular matrix elimination ends with, and $L$ holds the multipliers used to get there (ones on the diagonal). Given $A=LU$, each new right-hand side needs only a forward substitution $Lc=b$ and a back substitution $Ux=c$, about $n^2$ operations. The costly $\sim n^3/3$ elimination depends only on $A$, so it is paid once.

m3-l008-permutations-transposes.prompt: What goes wrong when a zero pivot appears, how do row exchanges fix it (giving $PA=LU$), and why is $P^{-1}=P^T$ for a permutation matrix?
m3-l008-permutations-transposes.rubric: Full credit requires: a zero pivot blocks elimination in that position, but a nonzero entry below can be swapped up if $A$ is invertible; $P$ records the swaps; $P$ has orthonormal columns (one 1 per row/column) so $P^TP=I$.
m3-l008-permutations-transposes.modelAnswer: If a pivot position holds zero, you cannot divide by it, but if the matrix is invertible some row below has a nonzero entry in that column; exchanging rows brings it up. The permutation matrix $P$ records all these swaps so that $PA=LU$ works. A permutation matrix has a single 1 in each row and column, so its columns are orthonormal and $P^TP=I$, meaning $P^{-1}=P^T$.

m3-l008-permutations-transposes.prompt: The cyclic permutation matrix $P=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ moves row 2 to row 1, row 3 to row 2 and row 1 to row 3. What is $P^{-1}$?
options: $P$ itself, since every permutation matrix is its own inverse.
It has no inverse, since $P$ has zeros on its diagonal.
$P^T$ (equal to $P^2$ here), since $P^TP=I$ for permutations.
$-P$, since undoing a rearrangement negates it.
m3-l008-permutations-transposes.explanation: The columns of a permutation matrix are orthonormal, so $P^TP=I$ and $P^{-1}=P^T$. Here $P^3=I$, so $P^{-1}=P^2=P^T$, which differs from $P$: only swaps of two rows are self-inverse.

m3-l008-permutations-transposes.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(1,2)$ entry of $(AB)^T$.
m3-l008-permutations-transposes.explanation: $AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&5\\4&11\end{pmatrix}$, so $(AB)^T=\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\5&11\end{pmatrix}$ and its $(1,2)$ entry is $4$. Equivalently $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$.

m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.prompt: Which of these subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is a subspace?
options: The plane $x+y+z=0$, which contains the origin and is closed under sums.
The plane $x+y+z=1$, since it is also a flat sheet in space.
The first octant ($x,y,z\ge0$), since sums of its vectors stay inside it.
The unit sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$, since it is symmetric about the origin.
m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.explanation: A subspace must contain $0$ and be closed under addition and scaling. $x+y+z=0$ passes both tests; the shifted plane misses the origin, the octant fails under multiplication by $-1$, and the sphere fails both.

options: $b=(1,2,4)$, since any vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be reached by two columns.
$b=(1,1,1)$, since it is perpendicular to the nullspace of $A$.
$b=(2,4,6)$, which equals $2(1,2,3)$ and so lies on the line spanned by both columns.
$b=(3,2,1)$, since its entries sum to 6, like the first column's entries.
m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.explanation: Both columns are multiples of $(1,2,3)$, so $C(A)$ is that line only. $(2,4,6)=2(1,2,3)$ is on it; the other vectors are not.

m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.prompt: The vector $b=(1,2,c)$ lies in the column space of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$ for exactly one value of $c$. Find $c$.
m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.explanation: The third column is the sum of the first two, so $C(A)$ is the plane of vectors $(x,y,x+y)$. For $b=(1,2,c)$ we need $c=1+2=3$.

m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.prompt: What does the column space $C(A)$ tell you about solving $Ax=b$, and why can't a plane that misses the origin, such as $x+y+z=1$, be a subspace?
m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $Ax=b$ is solvable exactly when $b$ is in $C(A)$, because $Ax$ is a combination of the columns; (2) a subspace must be closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so it must contain the zero vector (take the scalar 0); (3) the plane $x+y+z=1$ does not contain the origin, and the sum of two of its vectors lies on $x+y+z=2$, so it fails.
m3-l009-subspaces-column-space.modelAnswer: $Ax$ is always a combination of the columns of $A$, so $Ax=b$ has a solution exactly when $b$ lies in $C(A)$. A subspace must contain every combination of its vectors, in particular $0\cdot v=0$ and sums such as $v+w$. The plane $x+y+z=1$ misses the origin, and the sum of two of its points lies on $x+y+z=2$, so it is not a subspace.

m3-l010-nullspace-special-solutions.prompt: Find the dimension of the nullspace of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3&4\\2&4&6&8\\1&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l010-nullspace-special-solutions.explanation: Row 2 is twice row 1, so the rank is 2 and there are $4-2=2$ free variables, so $\dim N(A)=2$.

m3-l010-nullspace-special-solutions.prompt: The reduced row echelon form of $A$ is $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&3&0&2\\0&0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$. The special solution with free variables $x_2=0$, $x_4=1$ has what value of $x_3$?
m3-l010-nullspace-special-solutions.explanation: Set the free variables, then read off the pivot variables from $R$: $x_3=-4x_4=-4$ and $x_1=-3x_2-2x_4=-2$. So the special solution is $(-2,0,-4,1)$.

m3-l010-nullspace-special-solutions.prompt: Explain what the nullspace of $A$ tells you about the columns of $A$, why it is a subspace, and how the reduced form $R$ lets you read off its special solutions.
m3-l010-nullspace-special-solutions.rubric: Full credit requires: $x\in N(A)$ means a combination of the columns equals zero (so nonzero nullspace = dependent columns); closure under addition and scaling follows from linearity; free variables are set to 1/0 one at a time and the pivot variables are read off R (negatives of the free column entries).
m3-l010-nullspace-special-solutions.modelAnswer: A vector in the nullspace is a recipe for combining the columns of $A$ to get zero, so a nonzero nullspace means the columns are dependent. If $Ax=0$ and $Ay=0$ then $A(x+y)=0$ and $A(cx)=0$, so it is a subspace. In the reduced form $R$ each free column is a combination of the pivot columns; setting one free variable to 1 (others 0) and moving the pivot-column entries to the other side with a minus sign gives the special solutions, and all of $N(A)$ is their combinations.

m3-l011-particular-plus-nullspace-soluti.prompt: Two vectors $x_1$ and $x_2$ both solve $Ax=b$. What can you say about the difference $x_1-x_2$?
options: It solves $Ax=2b$, since the two right-hand sides add up.
It solves $Ax=b$ as well, since each of $x_1,x_2$ does.
It lies in the nullspace, since $A(x_1-x_2)=b-b=0$.
It must be zero, since a solution of $Ax=b$ is unique.
m3-l011-particular-plus-nullspace-soluti.explanation: By linearity $A(x_1-x_2)=Ax_1-Ax_2=b-b=0$. So every solution is one particular solution plus a nullspace vector: $x=x_p+x_n$.

m3-l011-particular-plus-nullspace-soluti.prompt: Solve $Ax=b$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&3&1&2\\0&0&1&4\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1,6)$, with the free variables $x_2=x_4=0$ (a particular solution). Give $x_1$.
m3-l011-particular-plus-nullspace-soluti.explanation: With $x_2=x_4=0$: $x_3=6$ from row 2, then $x_1+x_3=1$ gives $x_1=-5$. Adding any nullspace vector gives the complete solution.

m3-l011-particular-plus-nullspace-soluti.prompt: Explain why the complete solution to $Ax=b$ has the form $x=x_p+x_n$, and how the rank decides both solvability and the number of free parameters.
m3-l011-particular-plus-nullspace-soluti.rubric: Full credit requires: $A(x_p+x_n)=b+0$ and any two solutions differ by a nullspace vector; rank = number of pivots; solvable for all b if r=m, free parameters = n-r.
m3-l011-particular-plus-nullspace-soluti.modelAnswer: If $x_p$ solves $Ax=b$ and $x_n$ satisfies $Ax_n=0$, then $A(x_p+x_n)=b$; conversely the difference of two solutions is in the nullspace, so all solutions are $x_p$ plus the nullspace. The rank $r$ counts independent pivots: if $r=m$ every $b$ is reachable, otherwise only $b$ in the column space; and there are $n-r$ free variables, which sets the size of the family of solutions.

m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.prompt: $A$ is a $3\times5$ matrix with rank 3. What can you say about $Ax=b$?
options: Exactly one solution for every $b$, because the rank equals the number of equations.
It is always solvable (rank 3 equals the number of rows), with 2 free parameters in the complete solution.
Solvable only for some $b$, because there are more unknowns than equations.
Exactly two solutions for every $b$, one for each of the free variables.
m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.explanation: Rank $3 = m$ means the columns span all of $\mathbb{R}^3$ (always solvable) and $n-r=2$ free variables give a 2-parameter family $x_p+c_1s_1+c_2s_2$.

m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.prompt: Balancing $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6+a\,\text{O}_2\to b\,\text{CO}_2+c\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$ means finding the nullspace of the element-balance matrix. It has 3 rows (C, H, O) and 4 species columns and rank 3. What does that imply?
options: No balanced reaction exists, because the rank equals the number of elements.
Three independent balanced reactions exist, one for each element balanced.
A unique balanced reaction exists whose integer coefficients cannot be scaled at all.
The nullspace is one-dimensional: one balanced reaction exists, up to scale.
m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.explanation: $\dim N = n-r = 4-3 = 1$. Any multiple of the balanced equation is also balanced, which is why we fix the scale by demanding smallest integers.

m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.prompt: Balance $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6+a\,\text{O}_2\to 2\,\text{CO}_2+3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}$. How many moles of $\text{O}_2$ per mole of ethane ($a$)?
m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.explanation: Oxygen atoms: $2a = 2\cdot2+3 = 7$, so $a=3.5$. This is the nullspace vector $(1,3.5,2,3)$ of the balance matrix, scaled so ethane has coefficient 1.

m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.prompt: Explain why balancing a chemical equation is a nullspace problem, and what it means chemically when the nullspace of the element-balance matrix is two-dimensional rather than one-dimensional.
m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) put the species as columns and the elements as rows, with products counted negative; a balanced reaction is a coefficient vector $x$ with $Ax=0$; (2) the nullspace dimension is the number of independent balanced reactions, and any balanced reaction is a combination of basis vectors; (3) a two-dimensional nullspace means two independent reactions (e.g. extra species allow two separate balanced processes) so the balance is not unique up to scale.
m3-l012-rank-cases-balancing-reactions.modelAnswer: With species as columns and elements as rows, and products counted negatively, a balanced reaction is a vector $x$ with $Ax=0$. Every balanced reaction is a combination of nullspace basis vectors. If the nullspace is one-dimensional the balanced reaction is unique up to an overall scale; if it is two-dimensional there are two independent balanced reactions, and any balanced equation is a mix of them.

m3-l013-independence-and-basis.prompt: You have four vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Which statement is true?
options: They are independent as long as no two of them are parallel to each other.
They must be dependent, since the $3\times4$ matrix has a free column.
They are independent provided none of them is the zero vector itself.
They can form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$, since a basis may have any size.
m3-l013-independence-and-basis.explanation: Independence means $N(A)=\{0\}$. With $n=4>m=3$ there are at most 3 pivots, hence at least one free variable. Pairwise non-parallel is not enough, and every basis of $\mathbb{R}^3$ has exactly 3 vectors.

m3-l013-independence-and-basis.prompt: Find the dimension of the span of $(1,0,1)$, $(1,1,2)$ and $(0,1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$.
m3-l013-independence-and-basis.explanation: The third vector equals the second minus the first, so only two are independent: rank 2, a plane.

m3-l013-independence-and-basis.prompt: What is a basis, why does every basis of a given space contain the same number of vectors, and how does rank relate to the dimensions of the row space and column space?
m3-l013-independence-and-basis.rubric: Full credit requires: basis = independent and spanning; same size (dimension) because more vectors than the dimension would be dependent and fewer cannot span; rank = number of pivots = dim C(A) = dim C(A^T).
m3-l013-independence-and-basis.modelAnswer: A basis is a set of vectors that is independent (no redundancy) and spans the space (reaches everything). If one basis had more vectors than another, the extra ones would have to be dependent, and if it had fewer it could not span, so all bases have the same size, which defines the dimension. The rank is the number of pivots, and it equals both the dimension of the column space and of the row space.

m3-l014-rank-dimension-bases-from-pivots.prompt: After row reduction $A\to R$, a basis for the column space $C(A)$ is formed by:
options: The pivot columns of $R$, because row operations preserve the column space.
The pivot rows of $R$, rewritten as column vectors instead of rows.
The special solutions of $Ax=0$, which span the same space as the columns.
The columns of the original $A$ in the pivot positions, not those of $R$.
m3-l014-rank-dimension-bases-from-pivots.explanation: Row operations preserve the row space and the nullspace, but they change the column space (the columns of $R$ have different entries). The pivot positions tell you which original columns are independent.

m3-l014-rank-dimension-bases-from-pivots.prompt: A $3\times5$ matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0&1&3\\0&0&1&2&1\\1&2&1&3&4\end{pmatrix}$ has row 3 = row 1 + row 2. What is the dimension of its nullspace?
m3-l014-rank-dimension-bases-from-pivots.explanation: Rank is 2, so $\dim N(A)=5-2=3$. The row space and column space both have dimension 2.

m3-l014-rank-dimension-bases-from-pivots.prompt: Explain how row reduction to $R$ gives bases for the column space and the nullspace, and why the basis for $C(A)$ uses the pivot columns of the original $A$ rather than the columns of $R$.
m3-l014-rank-dimension-bases-from-pivots.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the pivot columns of $A$ are independent and every other column is a combination of them, so they form a basis of $C(A)$; (2) the special solutions (one per free column) form a basis of $N(A)$; (3) row operations preserve the dependencies among the columns (the nullspace) but change the columns themselves, so $C(R)\ne C(A)$ in general.
m3-l014-rank-dimension-bases-from-pivots.modelAnswer: The pivot columns of $A$ are independent and every free column is a combination of them, so they are a basis for $C(A)$; the special solutions, one for each free variable, form a basis for $N(A)$. Row operations leave the nullspace unchanged and so preserve which columns depend on which, but they change the columns themselves, so the column space of $R$ is generally different from that of $A$: use the pivot columns of $A$.

m3-l015-four-subspaces-dimensions-bases.prompt: A $5\times8$ matrix has rank 3. What is the dimension of its left nullspace $N(A^T)$?
m3-l015-four-subspaces-dimensions-bases.explanation: $\dim N(A^T)=m-r=5-3=2$. Together: $\dim C(A)=3$, $\dim N(A)=5$, $\dim C(A^T)=3$, $\dim N(A^T)=2$.

m3-l015-four-subspaces-dimensions-bases.prompt: A $3\times5$ matrix has rank 2. Which statement about its four fundamental subspaces is correct?
options: $C(A)$ and $N(A)$ lie in $\mathbb R^3$ (dimensions 2 and 3); $C(A^T)$ and $N(A^T)$ lie in $\mathbb R^5$ (dimensions 2 and 1).
$C(A)$ and $N(A^T)$ lie in $\mathbb R^3$ (dimensions 2 and 1); $C(A^T)$ and $N(A)$ lie in $\mathbb R^5$ (dimensions 2 and 3).
$C(A)$ and $N(A^T)$ lie in $\mathbb R^3$ (dimensions 2 and 2); $C(A^T)$ and $N(A)$ lie in $\mathbb R^5$ (dimensions 2 and 3).
$C(A)$ and $N(A^T)$ lie in $\mathbb R^5$ (dimensions 2 and 3); $C(A^T)$ and $N(A)$ lie in $\mathbb R^3$ (dimensions 2 and 1).
m3-l015-four-subspaces-dimensions-bases.explanation: Columns of $A$ have 3 components, so $C(A)$ and $N(A^T)$ live in $\mathbb R^3$ with dimensions $r=2$ and $m-r=1$. Inputs $x$ have 5 components, so $N(A)$ and $C(A^T)$ live in $\mathbb R^5$ with dimensions $n-r=3$ and $r=2$.

m3-l015-four-subspaces-dimensions-bases.prompt: Explain why the row space and the column space of an $m\times n$ matrix have the same dimension $r$, and use that fact to get $\dim N(A)$ and $\dim N(A^T)$.
m3-l015-four-subspaces-dimensions-bases.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) elimination finds $r$ pivots; the pivot columns of $A$ are a basis for $C(A)$ and the nonzero rows of $R$ are a basis for $C(A^T)$, so both dimensions equal $r$; (2) $A$ has $n-r$ free variables, so $\dim N(A)=n-r$; (3) applying the same counts to $A^T$ (an $n\times m$ matrix of the same rank $r$) gives $\dim N(A^T)=m-r$.
m3-l015-four-subspaces-dimensions-bases.modelAnswer: Row operations do not change the row space, and $R$ has $r$ nonzero rows, which are independent, so $\dim C(A^T)=r$; the $r$ pivot columns of $A$ are independent and span $C(A)$, so $\dim C(A)=r$ too. The other $n-r$ columns are free, giving $n-r$ special solutions, so $\dim N(A)=n-r$. $A^T$ is an $n\times m$ matrix of rank $r$, so its nullspace $N(A^T)$ has dimension $m-r$.

m3-l015b-bases-four-subspaces-from-r-and.prompt: Row-reducing $A$ to $R=EA$ leaves some zero rows at the bottom of $R$. The matching rows of $E$ give a basis for which subspace?
options: The left nullspace $N(A^T)$, since each such row $y^T$ satisfies $y^TA=0$.
The nullspace $N(A)$, because the zero rows of $R$ show which inputs vanish.
The column space $C(A)$, because those rows of $E$ come directly from $A$.
The row space $C(A^T)$, because row operations never change the row space.
m3-l015b-bases-four-subspaces-from-r-and.explanation: A zero row of $EA$ means $(\text{row of }E)\cdot A=0$, i.e. a vector with $y^TA=0$. These are exactly the left-nullspace vectors, and there are $m-r$ of them.

m3-l015b-bases-four-subspaces-from-r-and.prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\\3&6\end{pmatrix}$ the left nullspace contains a vector of the form $y=(y_1,1,0)$. Find $y_1$.
m3-l015b-bases-four-subspaces-from-r-and.explanation: Row 2 minus 2 times row 1 is zero, so $y=(-2,1,0)$ satisfies $y^TA=0$. It is the second row of $E$ in $EA=R$.

m3-l015b-bases-four-subspaces-from-r-and.prompt: Describe how to find a basis for each of the four fundamental subspaces of $A$ from the reduced form $R$ and the elimination matrix $E$ with $EA=R$.
m3-l015b-bases-four-subspaces-from-r-and.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) bases for $C(A)$ from the pivot columns of $A$, for $N(A)$ from the special solutions, and for $C(A^T)$ from the nonzero rows of $R$; (2) a basis for $N(A^T)$ from the rows of $E$ that correspond to zero rows of $R$, since $y^TA=0$ there (found by row-reducing $[A\ I]$ to $[R\ E]$).
m3-l015b-bases-four-subspaces-from-r-and.modelAnswer: Pivot columns of $A$ give a basis for $C(A)$, the special solutions give $N(A)$, and the nonzero rows of $R$ give $C(A^T)$. Row-reducing $[A\ I]$ to $[R\ E]$ also produces $E$: a row of $E$ that gives a zero row of $R$ satisfies $y^TA=0$, so those $m-r$ rows form a basis for $N(A^T)$.

m3-l016-rank-nullity-rank-one-matrices.prompt: A reaction network has 6 species and its element-balance matrix has rank 3. How many independent balanced reactions (independent vectors of stoichiometric coefficients) can exist?
options: 6, one independent reaction for every species in the network.
9, the number of species plus the rank of the balance matrix.
3, the nullspace dimension $n-r=6-3$, one for each free variable.
0, because six unknowns cannot satisfy three constraints at once.
m3-l016-rank-nullity-rank-one-matrices.explanation: Balanced reactions are vectors with balance matrix times coefficients $=0$, so they form the nullspace of dimension $n-r = 6-3 = 3$.

m3-l016-rank-nullity-rank-one-matrices.prompt: A $100\times100$ matrix of rank 2 can be written as a sum of two rank-one pieces (column times row). How many numbers must you store for this representation?
m3-l016-rank-nullity-rank-one-matrices.explanation: Each rank-1 piece $uv^T$ needs $100+100=200$ numbers, so two pieces need 400 instead of 10,000 for the full matrix. This is the idea behind low-rank compression.

m3-l016-rank-nullity-rank-one-matrices.prompt: In your own words, explain why $r+(n-r)=n$ and how the four fundamental subspaces pair up inside $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{R}^m$.
m3-l016-rank-nullity-rank-one-matrices.rubric: Full credit requires: each of the $n$ input directions is either a pivot direction (carried to the column space, $r$ of them) or a free direction (sent to zero, $n-r$); row space (dim r) + nullspace (dim n-r) fill $\mathbb{R}^n$; column space (r) + left nullspace (m-r) fill $\mathbb{R}^m$.
m3-l016-rank-nullity-rank-one-matrices.modelAnswer: Of the $n$ columns, $r$ are pivot columns that give independent directions and $n-r$ are free columns that can be expressed in terms of them. The free columns are what give the nullspace dimension $n-r$, so rank plus nullity counts all $n$ inputs. On the input side the row space (dimension $r$) and nullspace (dimension $n-r$) together account for $\mathbb{R}^n$; on the output side the column space ($r$) and left nullspace ($m-r$) together account for $\mathbb{R}^m$.

m3-l017-orthogonal-complements.prompt: Why is every vector in the nullspace of $A$ perpendicular to every row of $A$ (and to the whole row space)?
options: The rows of $A$ are always independent of each other, so they sit at right angles.
The nullspace is defined as the set of vectors perpendicular to the columns.
$Ax=0$ says every row dotted with $x$ is zero, so $x$ is perpendicular to all rows.
$A$ is assumed to be an orthogonal matrix, so its rows and columns are perpendicular.
m3-l017-orthogonal-complements.explanation: Reading $Ax=0$ row by row gives $\text{row}_i\cdot x=0$ for every $i$. The row space is spanned by these rows, so $x$ is perpendicular to all of it.

m3-l017-orthogonal-complements.prompt: A subspace $V$ of $\mathbb R^6$ has dimension 2. What is the dimension of its orthogonal complement $V^\perp$?
m3-l017-orthogonal-complements.explanation: The dimensions of a subspace and its orthogonal complement add up to the dimension of the whole space: $\dim V+\dim V^\perp=6$, so $\dim V^\perp=4$.

m3-l017-orthogonal-complements.prompt: Why is every vector in the nullspace perpendicular to the row space, and why do the two together fill all of $\mathbb R^n$, so that they are orthogonal complements rather than merely orthogonal?
m3-l017-orthogonal-complements.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $Ax=0$ says each row dotted with $x$ is zero, so $x$ is perpendicular to every row and to all their combinations; (2) $\dim C(A^T)+\dim N(A)=r+(n-r)=n$; (3) orthogonal subspaces whose dimensions add to $n$ leave no room for anything else, so every vector of $\mathbb R^n$ splits uniquely into a row-space part and a nullspace part.
m3-l017-orthogonal-complements.modelAnswer: $Ax=0$ says that every row of $A$ has zero dot product with $x$, so $x$ is perpendicular to the whole row space. Since $r+(n-r)=n$ the two subspaces have dimensions that add to $n$; two orthogonal subspaces with that property leave no direction uncovered, so every vector of $\mathbb R^n$ is uniquely a row-space part plus a nullspace part.

m3-l018-row-null-decomposition-ata.prompt: $A$ is $5\times3$ and its columns are linearly dependent. What can you say about the $3\times3$ matrix $A^TA$?
options: It is singular, since $A^TA$ has the same nullspace as $A$.
It is invertible, since any square symmetric matrix has an inverse.
It is invertible, since $A^T$ has independent rows even when $A$ does not.
It is undefined, since $A$ is not square and cannot be multiplied by $A^T$.
m3-l018-row-null-decomposition-ata.explanation: If $Ax=0$ then $A^TAx=0$, and conversely $A^TAx=0\Rightarrow x^TA^TAx=\|Ax\|^2=0$. So $N(A^TA)=N(A)$, and $A^TA$ is invertible exactly when $A$ has independent columns.

m3-l018-row-null-decomposition-ata.prompt: Take $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=(3,1)$. Split $x=x_r+x_n$ (row-space part plus nullspace part). Give the length $|x_n|$ of the nullspace component.
m3-l018-row-null-decomposition-ata.explanation: The row space is the line through $(1,1)$: $x_r=(2,2)$. The remainder $x_n=(1,-1)$ satisfies $Ax_n=0$, with length $\sqrt2\approx1.414$. $A$ sends $x$ to $Ax=4=Ax_r$; the nullspace part is invisible to $A$.

m3-l018-row-null-decomposition-ata.prompt: Describe what a matrix $A$ does to the row-space part and to the nullspace part of an input vector $x$, and why this means each output $b$ in the column space has exactly one row-space preimage.
m3-l018-row-null-decomposition-ata.rubric: Full credit requires: $x=x_r+x_n$ with $x_r\perp x_n$; $A x_n = 0$ so only $x_r$ matters; $A$ maps the row space one-to-one onto the column space (invertible between them), so each $b$ in $C(A)$ comes from exactly one row-space vector.
m3-l018-row-null-decomposition-ata.modelAnswer: Every input splits uniquely into a row-space piece and a nullspace piece that are perpendicular. $A$ annihilates the nullspace piece and carries the row-space piece to the output. Within the row space, $A$ is a one-to-one map onto the column space (both have dimension $r$), so each reachable output $b$ comes from exactly one vector in the row space, with all other solutions differing by a nullspace vector.

m3-l019-projection-onto-line-and-subspac.prompt: A projection matrix satisfies $P^2=P$. What is the physical or geometric reason?
options: $P$ is symmetric, and symmetry alone forces $P^2=P$ for every matrix.
After one projection the vector is already in the subspace.
Projecting twice returns the original vector, so $P$ undoes itself.
Every projection matrix has determinant 1.
m3-l019-projection-onto-line-and-subspac.explanation: $Pb$ is in $C(A)$, and $P$ leaves every vector of $C(A)$ unchanged. (Symmetry is a separate property, giving orthogonal projection, and a singular $P$ has determinant 0 unless $P=I$.)

m3-l019-projection-onto-line-and-subspac.prompt: Project $b=(1,2,3)$ onto the line through $a=(2,1,2)$. Give the second component of the projection $p$.
Using a picture, explain why the projection of $b$ onto the line through $a$ is $\dfrac{a^Tb}{a^Ta}\,a$, and what the leftover vector $b-p$ looks like.
m3-l019-projection-onto-line-and-subspac.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $p=\hat x a$ is the point on the line closest to $b$; (2) the error $e=b-\hat xa$ must be perpendicular to $a$, so $a^T(b-\hat xa)=0$; (3) solving gives $\hat x=a^Tb/a^Ta$, so $p=(a^Tb/a^Ta)a$ and $e\perp a$.
m3-l019-projection-onto-line-and-subspac.modelAnswer: The closest point on the line to $b$ is $p=\hat xa$, and the error $e=b-\hat xa$ must be perpendicular to $a$, otherwise one could move along the line to get closer. Setting $a^T(b-\hat xa)=0$ gives $\hat x=a^Tb/a^Ta$, so $p=\dfrac{a^Tb}{a^Ta}a$, and $e$ is perpendicular to the line.

m3-l019b-projection-onto-subspace.prompt: The matrix $P=A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$ projects onto $C(A)$. What does $P$ do to a vector $y$ in the left nullspace $N(A^T)$?
options: It returns $y$ unchanged, because $P^2=P$ means projections never change a vector.
It sends $y$ to a nonzero vector of $C(A)$, the closest point in the subspace.
It sends $y$ to $0$, because $y$ is perpendicular to every column of $A$.
It sends $y$ to $-y$, because $y$ is on the opposite side of the subspace.
m3-l019b-projection-onto-subspace.explanation: $Py=A(A^TA)^{-1}(A^Ty)=0$ because $A^Ty=0$. Projection keeps the $C(A)$ part of a vector and kills the part in $N(A^T)$; only vectors already in $C(A)$ are unchanged.

m3-l019b-projection-onto-subspace.prompt: Project $b=(6,0,0)$ onto the column space of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Give the third component of the projection $p$.
m3-l019b-projection-onto-subspace.explanation: $A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}3&3\\3&5\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^Tb=(6,0)$, so $\hat x=(5,-3)$ and $p=A\hat x=(5,2,-1)$. The third component is $-1$.

m3-l019b-projection-onto-subspace.prompt: Explain why the closest point $p=A\hat x$ in $C(A)$ to $b$ satisfies $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$, and how this gives the projection matrix $P$.
m3-l019b-projection-onto-subspace.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the error $e=b-A\hat x$ must be perpendicular to $C(A)$, i.e. to every column of $A$; (2) that says $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$, so $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$; (3) when $A^TA$ is invertible, $\hat x=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$ and $p=A\hat x=Pb$ with $P=A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$.
m3-l019b-projection-onto-subspace.modelAnswer: The closest point is the one for which the error is perpendicular to the whole subspace, so $e=b-A\hat x$ is orthogonal to every column of $A$: $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$. That is $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$, so $\hat x=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$ and $p=A\hat x=A(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb$, which is $Pb$.

m3-l020-normal-equations-geometry.prompt: In a least-squares fit $\min\|Ax-b\|^2$, what is true of the residual $e=b-A\hat x$?
options: It is parallel to $b$, since the fit just rescales the data vector.
It lies inside the column space of $A$.
It is the shortest vector with all of its components equal to each other.
It is perpendicular to every column of $A$, so $A^Te=0$.
m3-l020-normal-equations-geometry.explanation: The closest point $p=A\hat x$ in $C(A)$ is the projection of $b$, so the error $b-p$ is perpendicular to $C(A)$. That is $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$, the normal equations.

m3-l020-normal-equations-geometry.prompt: Explain in your own words why minimising $\|Ax-b\|^2$ leads to the normal equations $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$ and why this is a projection of $b$ onto the column space. Why is a calibration curve an example?
m3-l020-normal-equations-geometry.rubric: Full credit requires: closest point in a subspace is where the error is perpendicular to it; this gives $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$; the fitted values $A\hat x$ are the projection of the data vector onto the span of the model columns; calibration: data vector projected onto span{ones, concentration}.
m3-l020-normal-equations-geometry.modelAnswer: The set of all achievable predictions $Ax$ is the column space of $A$. The point in that subspace closest to the data $b$ is found by dropping a perpendicular, so the leftover error must be perpendicular to every column: $A^T(b-A\hat x)=0$, i.e. $A^TA\hat x=A^Tb$. A calibration fit has columns (ones, concentrations); the measured absorbances form a vector in a higher-dimensional space, and the fitted line is its projection onto the plane spanned by those columns.

m3-l020-normal-equations-geometry.prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$ (the matrix for fitting a line $C+Dt$ at $t=1,2,3$), give the $(2,2)$ entry of $A^TA$.
m3-l020-normal-equations-geometry.explanation: The $(2,2)$ entry of $A^TA$ is the dot product of the second column with itself: $1^2+2^2+3^2=14$.

m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.prompt: Fit a line $y=C+Dt$ by least squares to the points $(1,1),(2,2),(3,2),(4,4)$. Give the slope $D$.
m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.explanation: Solving $A^TA\hat x=A^Ty$ for $A=[1\;t]$ gives $C=0$, $D=0.9$ (the line passes through the origin). The residual vector is perpendicular to both the column of ones and the column $t$.

m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.prompt: A Beer-Lambert calibration through the origin $A_{\rm bs}=\varepsilon\ell\,c$ has data $c=0.1,0.2,0.4$ mM and absorbance $0.12,0.25,0.47$. Using one-column least squares, find $\varepsilon\ell$ in mM$^{-1}$.
m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.explanation: The projection onto a single column gives $\hat x=\dfrac{c\cdot A_{\rm bs}}{c\cdot c}=\dfrac{0.250}{0.21}\approx 1.190$ mM$^{-1}$. Calibration slopes are projections.

m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.prompt: To fit a parabola $y=C+Dt+Et^2$ to $m$ data points by least squares, what are the columns of the matrix $A$?
options: The data column $(y_i)$, $(t_i)$ and $(t_i^2)$, so that the data joins the fit.
A column of ones, $(t_i)$ and $(t_i^2)$, since the model is linear in $C,D,E$.
Only a column of ones and $(t_i)$, since a parabola cannot be fitted linearly.
The columns $(e^{t_i})$, $(t_i)$ and a column of ones, as curved fits need exponentials.
m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.explanation: The model $C+Dt+Et^2$ is linear in the unknowns $C,D,E$ even though it is quadratic in $t$, so the columns are the basis functions $1,\ t,\ t^2$ evaluated at the data points. The data vector $b=(y_i)$ is the right-hand side, not a column.

m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.prompt: In a Beer-Lambert calibration, explain why the least-squares fit is a projection of the absorbance vector onto the column space, and what the residual vector represents.
m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the model $A_{\rm bs}=\varepsilon\ell\,c$ makes the predictions a multiple of the concentration vector, i.e. a vector in the column space; (2) least squares picks the point in that space closest to the measured absorbance vector, which is the orthogonal projection; (3) the residual is the part of the data the model cannot reproduce (noise or deviations); it is perpendicular to the concentration column.
m3-l021-line-parabola-fitting-calibratio.modelAnswer: The model predicts absorbances $\varepsilon\ell\,c_i$, i.e. multiples of the concentration vector, so the predictions live in the column space of $A$. Least squares finds the vector in that space closest to the measured absorbances, which is the orthogonal projection. The residual is what the model cannot explain (noise and deviations from linearity), and it is perpendicular to the concentration column.

m3-l022-orthogonal-matrices-orthonormal-.prompt: If $Q$ has orthonormal columns and is square, what does multiplying a vector by $Q$ do?
options: It preserves lengths and angles (a rotation or reflection), since $Q^TQ=I$.
It preserves lengths but can change angles between different vectors.
It makes the components of any vector orthogonal to one another.
It scales every length by the factor $\det Q$ for any input vector.
m3-l022-orthogonal-matrices-orthonormal-.explanation: $Q^TQ=I$ gives $(Qx)\cdot(Qy)=x\cdot y$, so lengths and angles are unchanged. Also $\det Q=\pm1$, but that is a sign (orientation), not a scale factor.

m3-l022-orthogonal-matrices-orthonormal-.prompt: With orthonormal columns, least squares is simply $\hat x=Q^Tb$. For $q_1=(1,1,0)/\sqrt2$ and $b=(2,4,6)$, give $\hat x_1=q_1\cdot b$.
m3-l022-orthogonal-matrices-orthonormal-.explanation: $\hat x_1=(2+4)/\sqrt2=6/\sqrt2\approx4.243$. With orthonormal columns each coefficient is found independently, with no system to solve.

m3-l022-orthogonal-matrices-orthonormal-.prompt: Why does orthonormality make least-squares fitting almost trivial? What does $A^TA$ become when the columns of $A$ are orthonormal?
m3-l022-orthogonal-matrices-orthonormal-.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) orthonormal columns give $Q^TQ=I$; (2) so the normal equations $Q^TQ\hat x=Q^Tb$ reduce to $\hat x=Q^Tb$, each coefficient being a single dot product $q_i\cdot b$ with no system to solve; (3) the projection is $QQ^Tb$, the sum of the components of $b$ along each $q_i$.
m3-l022-orthogonal-matrices-orthonormal-.modelAnswer: With orthonormal columns $Q^TQ=I$, so the normal equations $Q^TQ\hat x=Q^Tb$ collapse to $\hat x=Q^Tb$: each coefficient is just the dot product $q_i\cdot b$ with no linear system to solve, and the projection is $QQ^Tb$, the sum of the components of $b$ along the $q_i$.

m3-l023-gram-schmidt-qr-factorisation.prompt: In $A=QR$ from Gram-Schmidt, why is $R$ upper triangular?
options: Gram-Schmidt processes the rows of $A$ from the bottom up to the top.
$R$ equals $Q^T$, and $Q$ happens to be lower triangular.
$q_k$ uses only $a_1,\dots,a_k$, so $a_k$ has no later $q_j$ parts.
The entries below the diagonal are cancelled to keep $Q$ orthogonal.
m3-l023-gram-schmidt-qr-factorisation.explanation: Each new $q_k$ lies in span$\{a_1..a_k\}$, hence each $a_k$ is a combination of $q_1..q_k$ only. The coefficients $r_{jk}=q_j^Ta_k$ vanish for $j>k$.

m3-l023-gram-schmidt-qr-factorisation.prompt: Apply Gram-Schmidt to $a_1=(1,1,0)$, $a_2=(1,0,1)$. In $A=QR$, what is $r_{22}$ (the length of the part of $a_2$ left after removing the $q_1$ component)?
Why does orthonormality make least-squares fitting almost trivial, and what does the matrix $R$ in $A=QR$ record?
m3-l023-gram-schmidt-qr-factorisation.rubric: Full credit requires: with $Q^TQ=I$, $A^TA$ becomes $I$ so $\hat x=Q^Tb$ (each coefficient is a dot product); R records the dot products $q_j^Ta_k$ (the Gram-Schmidt coefficients) and lengths, expressing the original columns in the new orthonormal basis.
m3-l023-gram-schmidt-qr-factorisation.modelAnswer: If the columns are orthonormal, $Q^TQ=I$, so the normal equations $Q^TQ\hat x=Q^Tb$ collapse to $\hat x=Q^Tb$: each coefficient is just the dot product of $b$ with one basis vector, with no coupling between them. In $A=QR$, Gram-Schmidt rewrites each original column $a_k$ in terms of the new orthonormal vectors, and $R$ stores those coefficients: the off-diagonal entries are the components removed, and the diagonal entries are the lengths of what was left.

m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.prompt: A $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ has $\det A=5$. What is $\det(2A)$?
options: $10$, because doubling the matrix just doubles its determinant.
$40$, since each of the 3 rows doubles and the determinant is linear in each: $2^3\cdot5$.
$25$, because the determinant is squared when the matrix is doubled.
$30$, because each of the three rows adds 1 to the scaling factor.
m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.explanation: The determinant is linear in each row separately, so scaling all 3 rows by 2 multiplies it by $2^3=8$: $8\cdot5=40$. In general $\det(cA)=c^n\det A$.

m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.prompt: In a $3\times3$ matrix, row 3 is replaced by (row 3) $-\,4\times$ (row 1). What happens to the determinant?
options: It is multiplied by $-4$, because a multiple of a row was subtracted.
It becomes $0$, because the new row 3 depends on row 1.
It is unchanged, because adding a multiple of one row to another preserves $\det$.
It changes sign, because two rows of the matrix were involved.
m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.explanation: By linearity in row 3, the new determinant is $\det A-4\det$(a matrix with rows 1 and 3 equal)$=\det A-0$. This is why elimination does not change the determinant.

m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.prompt: A $3\times3$ matrix $A$ has $\det A=5$. Matrix $B$ is obtained from $A$ by exchanging rows 1 and 3 and then multiplying row 2 by 3. What is $\det B$?
m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.explanation: A row exchange flips the sign ($-5$), and multiplying one row by 3 multiplies the determinant by 3, so $\det B=3\cdot(-5)=-15$.

m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.prompt: State the three defining properties of the determinant and show how they imply that a row exchange flips the sign and that $\det A=0$ for a matrix with two equal rows.
m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.rubric: Full credit requires: det I = 1; sign flips on exchange (or: linear in each row separately); stated consequences: two equal rows -> exchanging them changes nothing but flips sign, so det = -det = 0.
m3-l024-determinant-defining-properties.modelAnswer: The defining properties are: (1) $\det I = 1$; (2) the sign reverses when two rows are exchanged; (3) the determinant is linear in each row separately. If two rows are equal, exchanging them leaves the matrix unchanged but must flip the sign of the determinant, so $\det A=-\det A$, giving $\det A=0$. Row-subtraction then shows the determinant is unchanged by elimination, so it equals the product of the pivots.

m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.prompt: Why does $\det A=0$ exactly when $A$ is not invertible?
options: The determinant counts the nonzero entries, so it vanishes only for the zero matrix.
It measures how far $A$ is from symmetric, and singular matrices are skew.
It is defined as the largest eigenvalue.
$\det A=\pm$ product of pivots, and a singular matrix lacks a pivot.
m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.explanation: Elimination reduces $A$ to $U$ with $\det A=\pm\prod(\text{pivots})$ (the sign from row exchanges). A zero pivot means a dependent row, so $A$ is singular and the product vanishes.

m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.prompt: If $\det A=-16$ and $\det B=12$ for $3\times3$ matrices, what is $\det(A^{-1}B)$?
m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.explanation: $\det(A^{-1}B)=\det(A^{-1})\det B=\dfrac{12}{-16}=-0.75$, using $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ and $\det A^{-1}=1/\det A$.

m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.prompt: Compute $\det A$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&1\\1&1&0\\2&0&3\end{pmatrix}$ by elimination (the first pivot is zero, so a row exchange is needed).
m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.explanation: Exchange rows 1 and 2 (sign $-1$): rows $(1,1,0),(0,2,1),(2,0,3)$. Eliminate: row 3 minus 2 times row 1 gives $(0,-2,3)$, then plus row 2 gives $(0,0,4)$. Pivots $1,2,4$ give $8$, and the exchange gives $\det A=-8$.

m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.prompt: Explain why $\det(AB)=\det A\,\det B$ implies $\det A^{-1}=1/\det A$, and what this says about a singular matrix.
m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $AA^{-1}=I$, so $\det A\,\det A^{-1}=\det I=1$; (2) therefore $\det A^{-1}=1/\det A$, which only makes sense if $\det A\ne0$; (3) a singular matrix has $\det A=0$ and no inverse, so $\det A\ne0$ is the test for invertibility.
m3-l024b-determinant-pivots-product-rule.modelAnswer: Taking determinants of $AA^{-1}=I$ and using the product rule gives $\det A\cdot\det A^{-1}=\det I=1$, so $\det A^{-1}=1/\det A$. That requires $\det A\ne0$: a singular matrix has $\det A=0$, and no number can multiply 0 to give 1, which is consistent with it having no inverse.

m3-l025-computing-determinants-cofactors.explanation: The pivots are $2,-8,1$, with no row exchanges, so $\det A=2\cdot(-8)\cdot1=-16$.

m3-l025-computing-determinants-cofactors.prompt: Why does the big formula for a $3\times3$ determinant have exactly six terms?
options: There is one term for each entry of the matrix, so $9-3=6$ remain after cancellations.
One term for each of the $3!=6$ ways to pick one entry from every row and column.
There are two terms for each row of the matrix: one added and one subtracted.
One term for each of the six $2\times2$ minors that appear in the cofactor expansion.
m3-l025-computing-determinants-cofactors.explanation: Each term is a product of one entry from every row and every column, which corresponds to a permutation of the columns, and there are $3!=6$ permutations, each with a sign.

m3-l025-computing-determinants-cofactors.prompt: Explain how cofactor expansion along a row follows from the linearity of the determinant in each row, and why elimination is usually the better way to compute a large determinant.
m3-l025-computing-determinants-cofactors.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) write the chosen row as a sum of multiples of unit vectors and use linearity in that row, leaving $n$ smaller determinants (the cofactors, with sign $(-1)^{i+j}$); (2) cofactor expansion costs about $n!$ operations; (3) elimination costs about $n^3/3$ and the determinant is just the product of the pivots (with a sign for each row exchange).
m3-l025-computing-determinants-cofactors.modelAnswer: Splitting one row as $a_{i1}e_1+\dots+a_{in}e_n$ and using linearity in that row gives $\det A=\sum_ja_{ij}C_{ij}$, where each cofactor is a smaller determinant with sign $(-1)^{i+j}$. This costs of order $n!$ operations for an $n\times n$ matrix, whereas elimination takes about $n^3/3$ and gives the determinant as the product of the pivots, with a sign flip for each row exchange.

m3-l026-cramers-rule-cofactor-inverse.prompt: Why is Cramer's rule rarely used to solve large linear systems numerically?
options: It only works for $2\times2$ systems, since larger determinants are undefined.
It needs $n+1$ determinants, each costing about one full elimination.
It gives wrong answers whenever the determinant is small but nonzero.
It requires the coefficient matrix to be symmetric and positive definite.
m3-l026-cramers-rule-cofactor-inverse.explanation: Cramer's rule is exact and useful for formulas and small cases (symbolic work), but computing all those determinants is wasteful; elimination (LU) solves the system with a single factorisation.

m3-l026-cramers-rule-cofactor-inverse.prompt: Where does the formula $A^{-1}=C^T/\det A$ come from (what does $AC^T$ equal?), and what does it show about when $A^{-1}$ exists?
m3-l026-cramers-rule-cofactor-inverse.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) multiplying $A$ by the cofactor matrix transposed gives $\det A$ on the diagonal (cofactor expansion along a row) and $0$ off the diagonal (an expansion with a repeated row); (2) hence $AC^T=(\det A)I$; (3) dividing by $\det A$ gives the inverse, which therefore exists exactly when $\det A\ne0$.
m3-l026-cramers-rule-cofactor-inverse.modelAnswer: Row $i$ of $A$ times column $i$ of $C^T$ is the cofactor expansion of $\det A$ along row $i$. Row $i$ times column $j\ne i$ is the expansion of a matrix with two equal rows, which is $0$. So $AC^T=(\det A)I$, and $A^{-1}=C^T/\det A$, which exists exactly when $\det A\ne0$.

m3-l027-determinant-volume-jacobian.prompt: Why does the Jacobian determinant appear when you change variables in a multiple integral, e.g. $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$?
options: It is the average of the partial derivatives over the small region.
It makes the new coordinates orthogonal to the original ones.
It matters only for linear maps, never for curved coordinate systems.
It is the local factor by which the map scales area or volume.
m3-l027-determinant-volume-jacobian.explanation: A smooth map is locally linear (the Jacobian matrix) and $|\det|$ of a linear map is the volume scale factor. In polar coordinates $|\det J|=r$ because arc length grows with radius.

m3-l027-determinant-volume-jacobian.prompt: Find the volume of the parallelepiped whose edges are the rows $(1,2,0)$, $(0,1,3)$, $(2,0,1)$.
Explain geometrically why $|\det A|$ is the volume of the box spanned by the columns, and what $\det A=0$ says about that box.
m3-l027-determinant-volume-jacobian.rubric: Full credit requires: $|\det A|$ = volume of parallelepiped (unit cube maps to it); sign = orientation; zero determinant = columns dependent so the box is flat (zero volume, lies in a lower-dimensional space), consistent with singular matrix.
m3-l027-determinant-volume-jacobian.modelAnswer: $A$ maps the unit cube to the parallelepiped whose edges are the columns of $A$, and $|\det A|$ is the factor by which volume is scaled. The sign tells whether orientation is preserved. If $\det A=0$ the columns are dependent, so the box collapses into a lower-dimensional flat shape with zero volume; $A$ squashes space and cannot be undone, which is why it has no inverse.

m3-l028-eigenvalue-definition-characteri.prompt: A matrix $A$ has an eigenvector $x$ with eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$. What does $A$ do to the line through $x$?
options: It rotates the line by $90^\circ$ and doubles its length.
It maps the line to itself, reversing direction and stretching by $2$.
It collapses the line to the origin, since $\lambda$ is negative.
It maps the line to itself without any change of direction or length.
m3-l028-eigenvalue-definition-characteri.explanation: $Ax=-2x$ keeps $x$ on its own line, but the negative sign reverses its direction and $|\lambda|=2$ stretches it by a factor of 2.

m3-l028-eigenvalue-definition-characteri.prompt: Why are the eigenvalues of $A$ the roots of $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$, and how do you find the eigenvectors once an eigenvalue is known?
m3-l028-eigenvalue-definition-characteri.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $Ax=\lambda x$ means $(A-\lambda I)x=0$ has a nonzero solution; (2) that happens exactly when $A-\lambda I$ is singular, i.e. $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$; (3) for each root $\lambda$, the eigenvectors are the nonzero vectors of the nullspace of $A-\lambda I$, found by elimination.
m3-l028-eigenvalue-definition-characteri.modelAnswer: $Ax=\lambda x$ is $(A-\lambda I)x=0$, which has a nonzero solution only if $A-\lambda I$ is singular, i.e. $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$. This is a polynomial equation in $\lambda$. For each root, the eigenvectors are the nonzero vectors in the nullspace of $A-\lambda I$, which elimination finds.

m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.prompt: The rotation matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (a $90^\circ$ rotation) has what eigenvalues, and why?
options: $\pm i$: every real vector is turned, so none keeps its direction.
$+1$ and $-1$, one for each of the two directions it rotates.
Both $0$, since the matrix is singular and has zero trace.
$1$ twice, since a rotation preserves the length of every vector.
m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.explanation: $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2+1=0$. There is no real vector with $Ax=\lambda x$ because $A$ rotates every direction; the complex eigenvalues $\pm i$ encode the rotation. Length preservation shows $|\lambda|=1$, not $\lambda=1$.

m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.prompt: In Hückel theory, the secular equation $\det(H-E\,I)=0$ is an eigenvalue problem. What do the eigenvectors represent?
options: The number of electrons that occupy each of the molecular orbitals.
The bond lengths between neighbouring atoms in the conjugated chain.
The LCAO coefficients of each carbon $p$ orbital in each molecular orbital.
The nuclear charges of the atoms, which set the orbital energies.
m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.explanation: Eigenvalues are the orbital energies $E=\alpha+x\beta$; each eigenvector lists the atomic-orbital coefficients $c_i$ of the molecular orbital with that energy. Electron occupation is filled in afterwards.

m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.prompt: A $3\times3$ matrix has eigenvalues $2$ and $3$ and its trace is $10$. What is its determinant?
m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.explanation: The trace equals the sum of eigenvalues, so the third is $10-2-3=5$. The determinant is the product: $2\cdot3\cdot5=30$.

m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.prompt: Explain the geometric meaning of an eigenvector, and what complex eigenvalues or a defective matrix tell you about the transformation.
m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.rubric: Full credit requires: eigenvector keeps its direction (only stretched/flipped by lambda); complex eigenvalues = rotation component (no real invariant direction); defective = repeated eigenvalue with too few independent eigenvectors so no eigenbasis (shear-like).
m3-l029-trace-determinant-complex-huckel.modelAnswer: An eigenvector is a direction that the matrix only stretches (or flips) by the factor $\lambda$ without turning it. If the matrix rotates every real direction, as a rotation does, there are no real eigenvectors and the eigenvalues are complex, carrying the rotation angle and scale. A defective matrix has a repeated eigenvalue but too few independent eigenvectors, so there is no full eigenbasis; a shear is the typical example.

m3-l030-diagonalisation-powers-of-a.prompt: Which of these matrices cannot be diagonalised?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, because its eigenvalue 2 is repeated.
$\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, because its diagonal entries are zero.
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, which has only one eigenvector.
$\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, because one eigenvalue is negative.
m3-l030-diagonalisation-powers-of-a.explanation: A matrix is diagonalisable exactly when it has $n$ independent eigenvectors. A repeated eigenvalue is not the problem ($2I$ is already diagonal); the shear has $A-I$ of rank 1, giving only one eigenvector.

m3-l030-diagonalisation-powers-of-a.prompt: The matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $3$ and $2$ with eigenvectors $(1,0)$ and $(1,-1)$. Use $A^k=S\Lambda^kS^{-1}$ to find the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^5$.
Explain why $A^k=S\Lambda^kS^{-1}$ makes powers of $A$ easy, and what goes wrong if $A$ does not have $n$ independent eigenvectors.
m3-l030-diagonalisation-powers-of-a.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $A^k=(S\Lambda S^{-1})^k=S\Lambda^kS^{-1}$ because the inner $S^{-1}S$ factors cancel; (2) $\Lambda^k$ just raises each diagonal entry to the $k$-th power; (3) without a full set of independent eigenvectors $S$ is not invertible, so $A$ cannot be diagonalised (e.g. a Jordan block).
m3-l030-diagonalisation-powers-of-a.modelAnswer: In $(S\Lambda S^{-1})^k$ every inner $S^{-1}S$ cancels, leaving $S\Lambda^kS^{-1}$, and $\Lambda^k$ is just the diagonal of $\lambda_i^k$: no repeated matrix multiplication. This needs $n$ independent eigenvectors so that $S$ is invertible; a defective matrix such as $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has too few and cannot be diagonalised.

m3-l030b-linear-recurrences-fibonacci.prompt: Using $A=S\Lambda S^{-1}$ for the Fibonacci matrix, $F_k=(\varphi^k-\psi^k)/\sqrt5$. Estimate $F_{30}$ (use $\varphi^{30}/\sqrt5$, rounded).
m3-l030b-linear-recurrences-fibonacci.explanation: $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2\approx1.618$ is the dominant eigenvalue, and $\varphi^{30}/\sqrt5\approx832{,}040$ (the $\psi^k$ term is negligible). Growth rate is set by the largest eigenvalue.

m3-l030b-linear-recurrences-fibonacci.prompt: For the Fibonacci system $u_{k+1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}u_k$ the eigenvalues are $\varphi\approx1.618$ and $\psi\approx-0.618$. What does $F_{k+1}/F_k$ approach as $k\to\infty$?
options: $\psi\approx-0.618$, the smaller eigenvalue, because it controls the long-time behaviour.
$\varphi\approx1.618$, the dominant eigenvalue, because the other term dies out.
$1$, because each term is the sum of the two terms before it.
$2$, because each term roughly doubles the previous one.
m3-l030b-linear-recurrences-fibonacci.explanation: $F_k=(\varphi^k-\psi^k)/\sqrt5$ and $|\psi|<1$, so $\psi^k\to0$ and $F_{k+1}/F_k\to\varphi$, the golden ratio.

m3-l030b-linear-recurrences-fibonacci.prompt: Show how the recurrence $F_{k+2}=F_{k+1}+F_k$ becomes a first-order system $u_{k+1}=Au_k$, and explain how the eigenvalues of $A$ give a closed form for $F_k$ and its growth rate.
m3-l030b-linear-recurrences-fibonacci.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $u_k=(F_{k+1},F_k)$ and $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (adding the trivial equation $F_{k+1}=F_{k+1}$); (2) expand $u_0=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ so $u_k=c_1\lambda_1^kx_1+c_2\lambda_2^kx_2$ with $\lambda=(1\pm\sqrt5)/2$; (3) $F_k$ grows like $\varphi^k$ because the other eigenvalue has size less than 1.
m3-l030b-linear-recurrences-fibonacci.modelAnswer: Let $u_k=(F_{k+1},F_k)$. Then $F_{k+2}=F_{k+1}+F_k$ and $F_{k+1}=F_{k+1}$ give $u_{k+1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}u_k$. Its eigenvalues are $\lambda=(1\pm\sqrt5)/2$; writing $u_0$ as a combination of the eigenvectors gives $u_k=c_1\lambda_1^kx_1+c_2\lambda_2^kx_2$, so $F_k=(\varphi^k-\psi^k)/\sqrt5$. Since $|\psi|<1$, $F_k$ grows like $\varphi^k/\sqrt5$.

m3-l031-convergence-markov-matrices.prompt: Why does repeatedly applying a Markov (probability-conserving) matrix $A^kx_0$ settle to a steady state?
options: The eigenvalue-1 part survives while the other parts decay away.
Every entry of $A^k$ shrinks to zero, leaving the zero distribution.
All other eigenvalues are exactly zero except for one very large one.
$A^k$ eventually equals the identity matrix, freezing any distribution.
m3-l031-convergence-markov-matrices.explanation: $A^kx_0=\sum c_i\lambda_i^kx_i$. With $\lambda_1=1$ and $|\lambda_{i>1}|<1$ only the first term remains: the steady-state distribution (also the equilibrium populations of a kinetic scheme).

m3-l031-convergence-markov-matrices.prompt: A two-state system hops with transition matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}0.9&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{pmatrix}$ (columns sum to 1). In the long-time steady state, what fraction of the population is in state 1?
m3-l031-convergence-markov-matrices.explanation: The eigenvalue-1 eigenvector satisfies $0.1x_1=0.2x_2$, so $x=(2,1)$ normalised to sum 1 is $(2/3,1/3)$. The fraction is $0.667$.

m3-l031-convergence-markov-matrices.prompt: Explain why $A^k=S\Lambda^kS^{-1}$ makes powers easy, and how the sizes of the eigenvalues decide whether $A^kx$ grows, decays or settles.
m3-l031-convergence-markov-matrices.rubric: Full credit requires: in the eigenbasis A acts independently on each coordinate, so powers just raise each eigenvalue to k; $A^kx=\sum c_i\lambda_i^kx_i$; decays if all $|\lambda|<1$, grows if any $|\lambda|>1$, settles if the largest is exactly 1 and others are smaller.
m3-l031-convergence-markov-matrices.modelAnswer: Writing $x$ in the eigenvector basis, $A$ just multiplies each component by its eigenvalue, so applying $A$ $k$ times multiplies by $\lambda_i^k$: $A^kx=\sum c_i\lambda_i^kx_i$. The terms with $|\lambda_i|<1$ decay, those with $|\lambda_i|>1$ grow, and the largest eigenvalue eventually dominates; if it is exactly 1 and the rest are smaller, the vector converges to a steady state.

m3-l032-linear-ode-systems-eigenvalues-s.prompt: The system $\dot u=Au$ has eigenvalues $-1\pm2i$. How do solutions behave?
options: They spiral outward, growing exponentially while they oscillate.
They oscillate forever with constant amplitude, as for a centre.
They decay smoothly without oscillating.
They spiral into the origin, decaying like $e^{-t}$ while oscillating.
m3-l032-linear-ode-systems-eigenvalues-s.explanation: $e^{(-1\pm2i)t}=e^{-t}(\cos2t\pm i\sin2t)$: the imaginary part gives oscillation and the real part gives the decay. Stability depends on the real parts of the eigenvalues.

m3-l032-linear-ode-systems-eigenvalues-s.prompt: For $\dot u=Au$, how do the eigenvalues of $A$ determine whether solutions decay, grow or oscillate? Contrast real eigenvalues, a complex pair with negative real part, and a pair with positive real part.
m3-l032-linear-ode-systems-eigenvalues-s.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) solutions are combinations of $e^{\lambda_it}x_i$; (2) real negative eigenvalues give decay, a positive real eigenvalue gives growth; (3) a complex pair $\alpha\pm i\beta$ gives oscillation at $\beta$ inside an envelope $e^{\alpha t}$, decaying if $\alpha<0$ and growing if $\alpha>0$; stability needs every $\operatorname{Re}\lambda<0$.
m3-l032-linear-ode-systems-eigenvalues-s.modelAnswer: Each eigenpair contributes $c_ie^{\lambda_it}x_i$. A negative real $\lambda$ decays, a positive one grows. A complex pair $\alpha\pm i\beta$ gives oscillation at frequency $\beta$ inside an envelope $e^{\alpha t}$: a spiral into the origin if $\alpha<0$, out of it if $\alpha>0$. The system is stable when every eigenvalue has negative real part.

m3-l033-matrix-exponential-second-order-.prompt: For the consecutive first-order reactions $A\xrightarrow{k_1}B\xrightarrow{k_2}C$ written as $\dot u=Au$ (with $u=[A,B,C]$), what are the eigenvalues of $A$?
options: $k_1$, $k_2$ and $k_1+k_2$, the positive rates of the three steps.
$-k_1$, $-k_2$ and $0$, the zero being the all-$C$ end state.
$-k_1-k_2$ only, since the three concentrations decay together.
m3-l033-matrix-exponential-second-order-.explanation: The matrix is lower triangular with diagonal $-k_1,-k_2,0$. The rate constants are decay rates (negative eigenvalues), and the zero eigenvalue reflects conservation of total material, with the steady state being pure $C$.

m3-l033-matrix-exponential-second-order-.prompt: Turn $y''+3y'+2y=0$, $y(0)=1$, $y'(0)=0$ into a first-order system with $u=(y,y')$ and find $y(1)$.
Explain why $e^{At}=Se^{\Lambda t}S^{-1}$ solves $\dot u=Au$ and how the eigenvalues determine stability.
m3-l033-matrix-exponential-second-order-.rubric: Full credit requires: power series of $e^{At}$ and $A=S\Lambda S^{-1}$ gives $S e^{\Lambda t}S^{-1}$ (or direct: each eigenvector evolves independently as $e^{\lambda t}$); stability iff all real parts negative; zero real part = neutral (oscillation or constant), any positive real part = growth.
m3-l033-matrix-exponential-second-order-.modelAnswer: In the eigenbasis the system decouples into independent equations $\dot c_i=\lambda_ic_i$, each solved by $e^{\lambda_it}$; transforming back gives $u(t)=Se^{\Lambda t}S^{-1}u(0)=e^{At}u(0)$ (equivalently, substitute $A=S\Lambda S^{-1}$ into the power series of $e^{At}$). Every mode behaves as $e^{\lambda t}$, so the system decays to zero if all eigenvalues have negative real parts and blows up if any has a positive real part; the imaginary parts only add oscillation.

m3-l034-spectral-theorem-principal-axes.prompt: The quadratic form $x^TSx=1$ has $S$ with eigenvalues $1$ and $4$. What is its shape?
options: An ellipse with semi-axes $1$ and $4$ along the eigenvectors.
A hyperbola, since the two eigenvalues are different from each other.
An ellipse with semi-axes $1$ and $1/2$ along the eigenvectors.
A circle, since $S$ is symmetric and so has no preferred directions.
m3-l034-spectral-theorem-principal-axes.explanation: In the eigenbasis, $\lambda_1y_1^2+\lambda_2y_2^2=1$ has semi-axes $1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}$: a larger eigenvalue gives a shorter axis. Both eigenvalues positive gives an ellipse.

m3-l034-spectral-theorem-principal-axes.prompt: Why are the eigenvectors of a real symmetric matrix for different eigenvalues orthogonal, and why does that matter for normal modes of a molecule?
m3-l034-spectral-theorem-principal-axes.rubric: Full credit requires: argument $\lambda_1 x_1\cdot x_2=Sx_1\cdot x_2=x_1\cdot Sx_2=\lambda_2x_1\cdot x_2$ so $(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)x_1\cdot x_2=0$; consequence: independent, non-interacting modes, each oscillating at its own frequency; eigenvalues give $\omega^2$.
m3-l034-spectral-theorem-principal-axes.modelAnswer: Using symmetry, $\lambda_1(x_1\cdot x_2)=(Sx_1)\cdot x_2=x_1\cdot(Sx_2)=\lambda_2(x_1\cdot x_2)$, so if $\lambda_1\ne\lambda_2$ the dot product must be zero. For vibrations this means the normal modes form an orthogonal set of independent motions: energy put into one mode stays in it, each mode oscillating at its own frequency $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda/m}$, and any motion is a superposition of them.

m3-l034-spectral-theorem-principal-axes.prompt: A symmetric matrix has eigenvalues $3$ and $1$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $q_1=(1,1)/\sqrt2$ and $q_2=(1,-1)/\sqrt2$. Using $S=3q_1q_1^T+1\,q_2q_2^T$, find the $(1,2)$ entry of $S$.
m3-l034-spectral-theorem-principal-axes.explanation: $q_1q_1^T=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $q_2q_2^T=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, so the $(1,2)$ entry is $3\cdot\tfrac12+1\cdot(-\tfrac12)=1$, giving $S=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$.

m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.prompt: Two identical masses on springs have force-constant matrix $K=k\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with eigenvalues $k$ (vector $(1,1)$) and $3k$ (vector $(1,-1)$). Which statement is right?
options: The out-of-phase $(1,-1)$ mode is faster, and the two modes are orthogonal.
The in-phase $(1,1)$ mode is faster.
Both modes share one frequency.
