The $(1,-1)$ mode is faster, but the modes are not orthogonal because of the coupling.
m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.explanation: $\omega^2=\lambda/m$, so the larger eigenvalue $3k$ is the faster mode: the middle spring is stretched and compressed, so the restoring force is larger. The spectral theorem guarantees orthogonal eigenvectors for symmetric $K$.

m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.prompt: A symmetric coupled-oscillator problem has $K=k\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ with $k=100$ N/m and masses $m=0.5$ kg each. Find the angular frequency $\omega$ of the out-of-phase mode in rad/s.
m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.explanation: The eigenvalue is $3k=300$ N/m, so $\omega=\sqrt{300/0.5}=\sqrt{600}\approx24.5$ rad/s. (The in-phase mode has $\omega=\sqrt{200}\approx14.1$ rad/s.)

m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.prompt: The Hückel matrix for the allyl system is $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\1&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$ (in units of $\beta$). Give the largest eigenvalue.
m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.explanation: The eigenvalues are $\sqrt2,0,-\sqrt2$, giving orbital energies $\alpha+\sqrt2\beta$, $\alpha$, $\alpha-\sqrt2\beta$. The largest eigenvalue is $\sqrt2\approx1.414$ (the bonding orbital, since $\beta<0$).

m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.prompt: Explain why diagonalising the force-constant matrix gives the normal modes of a molecule, and how this parallels the Hückel orbitals being eigenvectors of the Hückel matrix.
m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the equations of motion are $m\ddot x=-Kx$ with $K$ real symmetric, so $K$ has orthonormal eigenvectors; (2) in the eigenvector (mode) coordinates the equations decouple into independent oscillators with $\omega^2=\lambda/m$; (3) likewise the Hückel Hamiltonian is a real symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues are orbital energies and whose orthonormal eigenvectors are the LCAO coefficients of the molecular orbitals.
m3-l035-normal-modes-huckel-spectral.modelAnswer: With $m\ddot x=-Kx$ and $K$ real symmetric, the orthonormal eigenvectors of $K$ are independent patterns of motion: in those coordinates each mode is a decoupled oscillator with $\omega^2=\lambda/m$. The Hückel matrix is likewise real symmetric: its eigenvalues are the orbital energies and its orthonormal eigenvectors are the LCAO coefficients of the molecular orbitals.

m3-l036-positive-definite-tests.prompt: Which of these symmetric matrices is positive definite?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, since all of its entries are positive.
$\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, with eigenvalues $1,3$ and pivots $2,1.5$.
$\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, since its entries are positive and increasing.
$\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, since its determinant $2$ is positive.
m3-l036-positive-definite-tests.explanation: Positive entries are not enough: the second and third matrices have determinants $-3$ and $-1$ (a negative eigenvalue). The last has $\det>0$ but both eigenvalues negative. Positive definite needs all eigenvalues (or pivots) positive.

m3-l036-positive-definite-tests.prompt: For the symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix}$, elimination gives pivots $2,\ 3/2,\ ?$. What is the third pivot?
m3-l036-positive-definite-tests.explanation: The pivots are $2,\tfrac32,\tfrac43$, all positive, so the matrix is positive definite. The product $2\cdot\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac43=4=\det$.

m3-l036-positive-definite-tests.prompt: Why is $A^TA$ always positive semidefinite, and why is that relevant to least-squares fitting?
m3-l036-positive-definite-tests.rubric: Full credit requires: $x^TA^TAx=\|Ax\|^2\ge0$; positive definite when columns independent ($Ax=0$ only for $x=0$); the least-squares cost $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is a quadratic with Hessian $2A^TA$, so it has a unique minimum (a bowl) when A has independent columns.
m3-l036-positive-definite-tests.modelAnswer: For any $x$, $x^TA^TAx=(Ax)\cdot(Ax)=\|Ax\|^2\ge0$, so $A^TA$ is positive semidefinite; it is strictly positive when $Ax=0$ only for $x=0$, i.e. independent columns. The least-squares error $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is a quadratic function of $x$ with Hessian $2A^TA$, so independent columns make it a bowl with a single minimum at the solution of the normal equations.

m3-l037-hessian-minima-saddles-transitio.prompt: A critical point of a potential energy surface has a Hessian with eigenvalues $+2$ and $-3$ (in some units). What is the point?
options: A local minimum, because at least one eigenvalue is positive.
A local maximum, because the larger-magnitude eigenvalue is negative.
Inconclusive, because a Hessian alone cannot classify a critical point.
A saddle point, as for a chemical transition state.
m3-l037-hessian-minima-saddles-transitio.explanation: A minimum needs all Hessian eigenvalues positive, a maximum all negative, mixed signs give a saddle. A transition state is a first-order saddle with exactly one negative eigenvalue (the reaction coordinate).

m3-l037-hessian-minima-saddles-transitio.prompt: The quadratic form $f=x^2+4xy+c\,y^2$ has a minimum at the origin only if $c$ exceeds a threshold. What is that value of $c$?
m3-l037-hessian-minima-saddles-transitio.explanation: $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&c\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det=c-4$, which must be positive (with $S_{11}=1>0$), so $c>4$. At $c=4$ the form is only semidefinite.

m3-l037-hessian-minima-saddles-transitio.prompt: How do the eigenvalues of the Hessian at a critical point of a potential energy surface show whether it is a minimum, maximum or saddle point, and why does a transition state have exactly one negative eigenvalue?
m3-l037-hessian-minima-saddles-transitio.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) near a critical point $f\approx f_0+\tfrac12x^THx$, and in the eigenvector coordinates this is $f_0+\tfrac12\sum\lambda_iy_i^2$; (2) all positive eigenvalues give a minimum, all negative a maximum, mixed signs a saddle; (3) a transition state is a maximum along the reaction coordinate but a minimum in all other directions, so it has exactly one negative eigenvalue.
m3-l037-hessian-minima-saddles-transitio.modelAnswer: Near a critical point $f\approx f_0+\tfrac12x^THx=f_0+\tfrac12\sum\lambda_iy_i^2$ in the eigenvector coordinates $y$. All $\lambda_i>0$ means a minimum, all negative a maximum, and mixed signs a saddle. A transition state is the highest point along the reaction path but the lowest in every perpendicular direction, so its Hessian has exactly one negative eigenvalue.

m3-l038-hermitian-inner-product-complex-.prompt: For $z=(1,i)$, the plain transpose gives $z^Tz=1+i^2=0$ even though $z\ne0$. What fixes this?
options: Restrict attention to vectors whose components are all real numbers.
Use the conjugate transpose: $\|z\|^2=z^Hz=\sum|z_k|^2$.
Take the absolute value of $z^Tz$ after multiplying out the terms.
Use $z^Tz$ as before, but only for vectors normalised to unit length.
m3-l038-hermitian-inner-product-complex-.explanation: A length must be real and positive. Conjugating one factor makes each term $\bar z_kz_k=|z_k|^2\ge0$, so $z^Hz=0$ only for $z=0$. For $z=(1,i)$, $z^Hz=2$.

m3-l038-hermitian-inner-product-complex-.prompt: Why does the correct inner product of complex vectors put a complex conjugate on one factor, and what does it mean for two complex vectors to be orthogonal?
m3-l038-hermitian-inner-product-complex-.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a plain $z^Tz$ can be zero or complex for a nonzero $z$ (e.g. $(1,i)$), so it cannot define a length; (2) $z^Hz=\sum|z_k|^2$ is real and positive; (3) two vectors are orthogonal when $z^Hw=0$, which is a complex condition (both real and imaginary parts vanish).
m3-l038-hermitian-inner-product-complex-.modelAnswer: For $z=(1,i)$ the plain product $z^Tz=1+i^2=0$, so it cannot be a length. Conjugating one factor gives $z^Hz=\sum|z_k|^2$, which is real and positive. Orthogonality means $z^Hw=0$, a complex equation, so both its real and imaginary parts must vanish.

m3-l039-conjugate-transpose-bra-ket.prompt: In bra-ket notation, what matrix object is the bra $\langle\psi|$ when $|\psi\rangle$ is a column vector?
options: The plain transpose of the column, with no complex conjugation applied.
The complex-conjugate column, conjugated entry by entry but not turned.
The matrix inverse of the ket, chosen so that $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1$.
The conjugate-transpose row, so $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle=\psi^H\phi$.
m3-l039-conjugate-transpose-bra-ket.explanation: Bras are conjugate-transpose rows, so $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=\sum|\psi_k|^2$ is a probability-like norm. The inner product is conjugate-linear in the first slot, so $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle=\overline{\langle\phi|\psi\rangle}$.

m3-l039-conjugate-transpose-bra-ket.prompt: Why does the correct inner product for complex vectors use a conjugate, what rule replaces $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$, and how does it connect to bra-ket notation?
m3-l039-conjugate-transpose-bra-ket.rubric: Full credit requires: conjugate needed so that length squared is real/positive; $(AB)^H=B^HA^H$; $|\psi\rangle$ = column, $\langle\psi|$ = conjugate row; $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$ is the same Hermitian inner product (complex number, conjugate when swapped).
m3-l039-conjugate-transpose-bra-ket.modelAnswer: Without conjugation a nonzero complex vector can have zero or complex 'length', so we conjugate one vector: $\langle z,w\rangle=z^Hw$, giving $\|z\|^2=\sum|z_k|^2>0$. For products, $(AB)^H=B^HA^H$: transpose and conjugate. A physicist's ket $|\psi\rangle$ is the column, the bra $\langle\psi|$ is its conjugate-transpose row, and $\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$ is exactly $\psi^H\phi$, the overlap of two states.

m3-l039-conjugate-transpose-bra-ket.prompt: In bra-ket notation let $|\psi\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,\,i)^T$ and $|\phi\rangle=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,\,1)^T$. Find the probability $|\langle\psi|\phi\rangle|^2$.

m3-l040-hermitian-matrices-observables.prompt: Find the larger eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix $H=\begin{pmatrix}1&1-i\\1+i&2\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l040-hermitian-matrices-observables.explanation: Trace $=3$ and $\det=2-|1-i|^2=2-2=0$, so the eigenvalues are $0$ and $3$ (real, as Hermitian demands).

m3-l040-hermitian-matrices-observables.prompt: Explain why a Hermitian matrix has real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors, and why $e^{-iHt}$ is unitary when $H$ is Hermitian.
m3-l040-hermitian-matrices-observables.rubric: Full credit requires: $\lambda\|x\|^2=x^HHx$ is real since $(x^HHx)^*=x^HH^Hx=x^HHx$; orthogonality by the same swap argument; $U=e^{-iHt}$ has $U^HU=e^{iHt}e^{-iHt}=I$ (or eigenvalues $e^{-i\lambda t}$ of modulus 1).
m3-l040-hermitian-matrices-observables.modelAnswer: For $Hx=\lambda x$, the number $x^HHx=\lambda\|x\|^2$ equals its own conjugate because $H=H^H$, so $\lambda$ is real; the same swap shows eigenvectors with different eigenvalues are orthogonal. Writing $H=U\Lambda U^H$, $e^{-iHt}=Ue^{-i\Lambda t}U^H$ has eigenvalues $e^{-i\lambda t}$ of modulus one, and $(e^{-iHt})^H e^{-iHt}=e^{iHt}e^{-iHt}=I$, so it preserves probability.

m3-l040-hermitian-matrices-observables.prompt: A Hermitian matrix $H$ has two different eigenvalues $E_1\ne E_2$ with eigenvectors $v_1,v_2$. Which statement is true?
options: Both eigenvalues are real, but $v_1$ and $v_2$ need not be orthogonal.
$v_1$ and $v_2$ are orthogonal, but the eigenvalues can be complex.
$v_1^Hv_2=0$ and both eigenvalues are real, because $H=H^H$.
The eigenvalues are real and equal, because $H$ equals its conjugate transpose.
m3-l040-hermitian-matrices-observables.explanation: If $Hv=Ev$ then $E\,v^Hv=v^HHv=(H^Hv)^Hv=\bar E\,v^Hv$, so $E$ is real. For two eigenvalues, $(E_1-E_2)v_1^Hv_2=0$ forces orthogonality. These are the properties that make Hermitian matrices good observables.

m3-l041-unitary-matrices-time-evolution.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes quantum mechanics?
options: Observables are Hermitian, and time evolution is unitary.
Observables are unitary, and time evolution is Hermitian.
Both observables and time evolution are Hermitian matrices acting on states.
Observables can be any real matrix, and time evolution any invertible matrix.
m3-l041-unitary-matrices-time-evolution.explanation: Hermitian matrices have real eigenvalues, which are the possible measurement results. Unitary matrices preserve $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$, so $e^{-iHt/\hbar}$ keeps total probability equal to 1.

m3-l041-unitary-matrices-time-evolution.prompt: A spin starts in $|0\rangle$ and evolves under the unitary $U=e^{i\theta\sigma_x}=\cos\theta\,I+i\sin\theta\,\sigma_x$ with $\theta=\pi/6$. What is the probability to find it in $|1\rangle$?
m3-l041-unitary-matrices-time-evolution.explanation: $U|0\rangle=\cos\theta|0\rangle+i\sin\theta|1\rangle$, so $P(1)=\sin^2(\pi/6)=0.25$. Probabilities still add to 1 because $U$ is unitary.

m3-l041-unitary-matrices-time-evolution.prompt: Explain what it means for a unitary matrix to preserve the inner product, why every eigenvalue of a unitary matrix has modulus 1, and why that guarantees that total probability stays 1 during time evolution.
m3-l041-unitary-matrices-time-evolution.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $U^HU=I$ gives $(Uz)^H(Uw)=z^Hw$, so lengths and angles are preserved; (2) if $Uv=\lambda v$ then $\|Uv\|=|\lambda|\|v\|=\|v\|$, so $|\lambda|=1$; (3) the state evolves as $\psi(t)=U\psi(0)$ with $\|U\psi\|=\|\psi\|$, so the total probability $\|\psi\|^2=1$ is conserved.
m3-l041-unitary-matrices-time-evolution.modelAnswer: $U^HU=I$ means $(Uz)^H(Uw)=z^Hw$: inner products, and so lengths and angles, are unchanged. If $Uv=\lambda v$ then $\|v\|=\|Uv\|=|\lambda|\|v\|$, so $|\lambda|=1$. A state evolving as $\psi(t)=U\psi(0)$ therefore keeps $\|\psi\|^2=\sum|c_k|^2=1$ at all times: probability is conserved.

m3-l042-pauli-matrices-spin-nmr.prompt: The Pauli matrices are both Hermitian and unitary. What must their eigenvalues be?
options: $+i$ or $-i$, like a rotation through $90^\circ$ in the plane.
Any real numbers at all.
Only $+1$ or $-1$: real, and of modulus one.
$0$ or $1$, as for projection operators onto a subspace.
m3-l042-pauli-matrices-spin-nmr.explanation: Real and modulus 1 leaves $\pm1$. Hence a spin-1/2 measurement along any axis gives one of two outcomes (in units of $\hbar/2$).

m3-l042-pauli-matrices-spin-nmr.prompt: A proton in a field $B=9.4$ T has the two-level Hamiltonian $H=\tfrac12\hbar\gamma B\,\sigma_z$, so the two energy levels differ by $\hbar\gamma B$. With $\gamma=2.675\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}T^{-1}}$, find the resonance frequency $\nu=\gamma B/2\pi$ in MHz.
m3-l042-pauli-matrices-spin-nmr.explanation: The eigenvalues of $\tfrac12\hbar\gamma B\sigma_z$ are $\pm\tfrac12\hbar\gamma B$, so the splitting is $\hbar\gamma B=h\nu$ with $\nu=\gamma B/2\pi=2.675\times10^8\times9.4/(2\pi)\approx4.0\times10^8$ Hz $=400$ MHz: the '400 MHz' NMR spectrometer.

m3-l042-pauli-matrices-spin-nmr.prompt: Explain why the eigenvalues of $H=\tfrac12\hbar\gamma B\,\sigma_z$ are the two NMR energy levels, which spin states they belong to, and how their spacing sets the resonance frequency.
m3-l042-pauli-matrices-spin-nmr.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $\sigma_z$ is diagonal with eigenvalues $\pm1$ and eigenvectors $|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle$, so $H$ has energies $\pm\tfrac12\hbar\gamma B$; (2) these belong to the two spin states aligned or anti-aligned with the field; (3) a photon is absorbed when $h\nu$ equals the spacing $\hbar\gamma B$, so the resonance frequency is $\nu=\gamma B/2\pi$, proportional to the field.
m3-l042-pauli-matrices-spin-nmr.modelAnswer: $\sigma_z=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$ has eigenvectors $|\uparrow\rangle$ and $|\downarrow\rangle$, so $H$ has energies $\pm\tfrac12\hbar\gamma B$ for spin aligned or anti-aligned with the field. The levels are $\hbar\gamma B$ apart, and a photon is absorbed when $h\nu=\hbar\gamma B$, i.e. $\nu=\gamma B/2\pi$: the resonance frequency grows linearly with the magnetic field.

m3-l043-fourier-matrix-dft.prompt: What does it mean that $F_n/\sqrt n$ is a unitary matrix?
options: Its columns are orthonormal complex exponentials, so its inverse is $F^H$.
Its columns are real vectors of unit length that point along coordinate axes.
Its entries all have modulus $1/n$.
It is symmetric, so it is its own inverse and the transform is an involution.
m3-l043-fourier-matrix-dft.explanation: The columns $(1,\omega^k,\omega^{2k},\dots)/\sqrt n$ are orthonormal under the Hermitian inner product, so $F^HF=nI$. This is why Fourier expansion works like any orthonormal-basis expansion, and inverting costs the same as the forward transform.

m3-l043-fourier-matrix-dft.prompt: A signal $x_j=\cos(2\pi\cdot2\,j/8)$, $j=0..7$, is Fourier transformed with an 8-point DFT. What is the magnitude of the coefficient at frequency index $k=2$?
m3-l043-fourier-matrix-dft.explanation: $\cos$ is half of $e^{2\pi i2j/8}$ plus half of its conjugate; the DFT sums 8 terms of size $1/2$ aligned in phase, giving magnitude $8/2=4$ at $k=2$ (and $k=6$).

m3-l043-fourier-matrix-dft.prompt: Interpret the discrete Fourier transform as an expansion in an orthonormal basis: what are the basis vectors, and what do the Fourier coefficients of a signal measure?
m3-l043-fourier-matrix-dft.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the columns of $F_n/\sqrt n$ are the complex exponentials $(1,w^k,w^{2k},\dots)$ with $w=e^{2\pi i/n}$, which are orthonormal; (2) the coefficients are $c_k=\frac1n$ (or $1/\sqrt n$) times the inner product of the signal with the $k$-th exponential, found by $F^{-1}=F^H/n$; (3) $|c_k|$ measures how much of the signal oscillates at the $k$-th frequency.
m3-l043-fourier-matrix-dft.modelAnswer: The columns of $F_n/\sqrt n$ are the sampled complex exponentials $(1,w^k,w^{2k},\dots)$, $w=e^{2\pi i/n}$, and they are orthonormal, so $F^{-1}$ is just $F^H$ (up to scale). The DFT coefficient $c_k$ is the inner product of the signal with the $k$-th exponential, and $|c_k|$ measures how much of the signal oscillates at the $k$-th frequency.

m3-l044-fast-fourier-transform-algorithm.prompt: What is the key idea that lets the FFT compute an $n$-point DFT in about $n\log_2 n$ operations instead of $n^2$?
options: It discards the small Fourier coefficients and computes only the large ones.
It works only for real signals.
$F_n$ factors into sparse matrices built from half-size transforms.
It uses the inverse matrix.
m3-l044-fast-fourier-transform-algorithm.explanation: The FFT is exact, not approximate. Splitting by even/odd indices reduces one size-$n$ transform to two size-$n/2$ transforms plus $O(n)$ work, and recursion over $\log_2n$ levels gives $O(n\log n)$.

m3-l044-fast-fourier-transform-algorithm.prompt: Compare the cost of a direct DFT ($n^2$) with an FFT ($n\log_2n$) for $n=1024$. By what factor is the FFT faster?
Interpret the discrete Fourier transform as an expansion in an orthonormal basis, and say in words why splitting into even and odd samples saves work.
m3-l044-fast-fourier-transform-algorithm.rubric: Full credit requires: DFT coefficients = inner products with orthonormal complex exponentials (signal rewritten as a sum of them); even/odd split: two half-size DFTs reuse shared structure ($\omega^2$ is the primitive root for n/2), repeated recursively -> n log n.
m3-l044-fast-fourier-transform-algorithm.modelAnswer: The DFT finds how much of each complex exponential is in a sampled signal; because those exponentials form an orthonormal basis, the coefficients are just inner products and the original signal is recovered by summing the basis vectors back up. The FFT notices that the even-indexed and odd-indexed samples each form a half-size DFT using the same exponentials squared, so one size-$n$ transform becomes two size-$n/2$ transforms plus a linear pass; recursing $\log_2n$ times costs $n\log n$ instead of $n^2$.

m3-l045-svd-factorisation-geometry.prompt: Geometrically, what does $A=U\Sigma V^T$ do to the unit circle in $\mathbb{R}^2$?
options: A larger circle, scaled by the largest eigenvalue of $A$ in every direction.
An ellipse whose semi-axes are always the eigenvalues of $A$ itself.
A line segment of length $\det A$, since the matrix compresses the circle.
It becomes an ellipse whose semi-axes are $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$.
m3-l045-svd-factorisation-geometry.explanation: Every matrix maps the unit circle to an ellipse (possibly degenerate). The semi-axis lengths are the singular values, which agree with eigenvalues only for symmetric positive semidefinite matrices.

m3-l045-svd-factorisation-geometry.prompt: How do you obtain the singular values and right singular vectors of $A$?
options: From the eigenproblem of $A$ itself, where the eigenvalues are the $\sigma_i$.
From $A^TA$: its eigenvectors give $V$ and its eigenvalues give $\sigma_i^2$.
From the eigenproblem of $A+A^T$, which is always symmetric and real.
From the pivots that elimination finds when it reduces $A$ to echelon form.
m3-l045-svd-factorisation-geometry.explanation: $A^TA=V\Sigma^TU^TU\Sigma V^T=V\Sigma^2V^T$, a symmetric eigenproblem that exists for every matrix, even rectangular or defective ones. Then $u_i=Av_i/\sigma_i$.

m3-l045-svd-factorisation-geometry.prompt: Explain in words what $A=U\Sigma V^T$ does to a vector geometrically, and where the singular values and the matrices $U$ and $V$ come from.
m3-l045-svd-factorisation-geometry.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) $V^T$ rotates (or reflects) to the right-singular-vector axes, $\Sigma$ stretches each axis by $\sigma_i$, and $U$ rotates into the output space; (2) $V$ and $\sigma_i^2$ come from the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $A^TA$, and $U$ from those of $AA^T$ (or $u_i=Av_i/\sigma_i$); (3) the unit circle becomes an ellipse with semi-axes $\sigma_i$ along the $u_i$.
m3-l045-svd-factorisation-geometry.modelAnswer: $V^T$ rotates the input onto the orthonormal axes $v_i$, $\Sigma$ stretches the $i$-th axis by $\sigma_i$, and $U$ rotates the result into the output space, so a unit circle becomes an ellipse with semi-axes $\sigma_i$ along the $u_i$. The $v_i$ and $\sigma_i^2$ are the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of $A^TA$, and $u_i=Av_i/\sigma_i$.

m3-l046-svd-by-hand-four-subspaces.prompt: Find the largest singular value of $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$.
m3-l046-svd-by-hand-four-subspaces.explanation: $A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}25&20\\20&25\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $45$ and $5$, so $\sigma=\sqrt{45}\approx6.708$ and $\sqrt5$. Note $\sigma_1\sigma_2=15=|\det A|$.

m3-l046-svd-by-hand-four-subspaces.prompt: The rank-one matrix $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ has one nonzero singular value. What is it?
Explain how the SVD hands you orthonormal bases for all four fundamental subspaces.
m3-l046-svd-by-hand-four-subspaces.rubric: Full credit requires: first r columns of V = row space, remaining n-r = nullspace; first r columns of U = column space, remaining m-r = left nullspace; $Av_i=\sigma_iu_i$ ties them together.
m3-l046-svd-by-hand-four-subspaces.modelAnswer: In $A=U\Sigma V^T$, the first $r$ columns of $V$ (with nonzero $\sigma_i$) form an orthonormal basis for the row space, and the remaining $n-r$ columns span the nullspace since $Av_i=0$ there. Likewise the first $r$ columns of $U$ form a basis for the column space and the last $m-r$ for the left nullspace. $A$ maps $v_i\to\sigma_iu_i$, pairing a row-space direction with a column-space direction.

m3-l047-low-rank-approximation-pca.prompt: A data matrix has singular values $10, 5, 0.1, 0.01$. Why is the rank-2 truncation a good approximation?
options: The error is the next singular value, $0.1$, small against $10$ and $5$.
Because the first two singular values are both larger than one.
Because the rank-2 approximation is exact for any matrix with 4 columns.
Because the smallest singular values carry the main information in the data.
m3-l047-low-rank-approximation-pca.explanation: The truncated SVD $\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^T$ is the closest rank-$k$ matrix, with 2-norm error $\sigma_{k+1}$. Large singular values carry the dominant structure (e.g. component spectra); tiny ones are typically noise.

m3-l047-low-rank-approximation-pca.prompt: In a PCA of a spectral data set the singular values are $6,\,3,\,2$. What percentage of the total variance (sum of $\sigma_i^2$) does the first principal component capture?
m3-l047-low-rank-approximation-pca.explanation: Variance scales as $\sigma^2$: $36/(36+9+4)=36/49\approx73.5\%$. Two components capture $45/49\approx92\%$.

m3-l047-low-rank-approximation-pca.prompt: Describe the steps of PCA on a set of spectra (centre, SVD or covariance, principal components) and say what the singular values tell you about how many independent components a mixture data set contains.
m3-l047-low-rank-approximation-pca.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) subtract the mean spectrum from each spectrum; (2) take the SVD of the centred data matrix (equivalently eigendecompose the covariance matrix); the right singular vectors are the principal components; (3) the squared singular values give the variance carried by each component, so a sharp drop after $k$ values suggests about $k$ independent components (plus noise).
m3-l047-low-rank-approximation-pca.modelAnswer: Subtract the mean spectrum, then take the SVD of the centred data matrix; the right singular vectors are the principal components (the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix). The squared singular values give the variance along each component, so if they drop sharply after $k$ values, the mixtures are built from about $k$ independent component spectra, with the rest being noise.

m3-l048-pseudoinverse-condition-number.prompt: A matrix has singular values $1000$ and $0.001$. What does its condition number $\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}=10^6$ tell you?
options: It is invertible, with an inverse whose norm is exactly $0.001$.
It has rank $10^6$, which makes the system hugely over-determined.
Relative errors can be amplified up to $10^6$ times in the solution.
Computations are accurate, because the largest singular value is large.
m3-l048-pseudoinverse-condition-number.explanation: Dividing by $\sigma_{\min}$ magnifies tiny errors in the corresponding direction. Large condition numbers signal near-dependent columns (e.g. strongly overlapping spectra in a calibration).

m3-l048-pseudoinverse-condition-number.prompt: Compute the condition number $\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$ of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4.01\end{pmatrix}$ (nearly singular). Give the value to a few significant figures.
m3-l048-pseudoinverse-condition-number.explanation: The singular values are about $5.01$ and $0.002$, so the condition number is roughly $2.5\times10^3$. Nearly dependent columns make solving $Ax=b$ very sensitive.

m3-l048-pseudoinverse-condition-number.prompt: What does the pseudoinverse $A^+=V\Sigma^+U^T$ give you, and how would SVD or PCA help you analyse a set of spectra of mixtures?
m3-l048-pseudoinverse-condition-number.rubric: Full credit requires: $A^+b$ is the least-squares solution of smallest norm (inverts nonzero $\sigma$, ignores zero ones, lies in the row space); spectra: SVD/PCA finds a few dominant components (rank = number of independent species), the rest is noise; centre data first for PCA.
m3-l048-pseudoinverse-condition-number.modelAnswer: $A^+$ inverts $A$ only on the directions it actually uses (dividing by nonzero $\sigma_i$) and ignores the rest, so $A^+b$ is the least-squares solution that also has the smallest length, even when $A$ is rank-deficient or rectangular. For a data set of mixture spectra the SVD finds the few orthogonal spectral components that explain nearly all the variance; the number of large singular values estimates how many independent absorbing species are present, and the small ones are noise.

m3-l049-linear-transformations-matrix-of.prompt: Which of these maps of the plane to itself is NOT a linear transformation?
options: Rotation by $30^\circ$ about the origin of the plane.
Translation by $(1,0)$, which moves the origin so cannot be linear.
Orthogonal projection onto the $x$-axis of the plane.
Reflection across the line $y=x$ in the plane.
m3-l049-linear-transformations-matrix-of.explanation: Linearity requires $T(0)=0$ (and $T(cv)=cT(v)$, $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$). Translation moves the origin, so it fails; it is an affine, not linear, map.

m3-l049-linear-transformations-matrix-of.prompt: A linear transformation rotates the plane counterclockwise by $30^\circ$. What is the $x$-component of the image of the vector $(0,1)$?
m3-l049-linear-transformations-matrix-of.explanation: The second column of the rotation matrix is the image of $(0,1)$: $(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)=(-0.5,0.866)$, so the $x$-component is $-\sin30^\circ=-0.5$.

m3-l049-linear-transformations-matrix-of.prompt: Explain how to test whether a map $T$ is linear. Show why the shift $T(v)=v+(1,0)$ fails the test, while every $T(v)=Av$ passes.
m3-l049-linear-transformations-matrix-of.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) linearity means $T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w)$ and $T(cv)=cT(v)$ (together $T(cv+dw)=cT(v)+dT(w)$); (2) the shift fails, e.g. $T(0)=(1,0)\ne0$ or $T(2v)\ne2T(v)$; (3) $A(cv+dw)=cAv+dAw$ follows from the rules of matrix multiplication.
m3-l049-linear-transformations-matrix-of.modelAnswer: A map is linear if it respects addition and scaling: $T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w)$ and $T(cv)=cT(v)$. The shift fails because $T(0)=(1,0)$ is not the zero vector, and $T(2v)=2v+(1,0)\ne2T(v)$. Matrix maps pass because $A(cv+dw)=cAv+dAw$.

m3-l049b-matrix-of-t-in-bases.prompt: Let $D=d/dx$ act on polynomials of degree $\le2$ with basis $\{1,x,x^2\}$. The matrix of $D$ has columns $D(1),D(x),D(x^2)$ written in the basis. Give the entry in row 2, column 3.
m3-l049b-matrix-of-t-in-bases.explanation: $D(x^2)=2x=0\cdot1+2\cdot x+0\cdot x^2$, so column 3 is $(0,2,0)^T$ and the $(2,3)$ entry is 2. The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&2\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has nullspace spanned by the constant.

m3-l049b-matrix-of-t-in-bases.prompt: The linear map $T$ projects the plane onto the line $y=x$. Using the basis $v_1=(1,1)$, $v_2=(1,-1)$ for both input and output, what is the matrix of $T$?
options: $\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{pmatrix}$, the projection matrix in the standard basis.
$\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, keeping only the second basis vector.
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, keeping $v_1$ and killing $v_2$.
$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, since a projection does not change the plane.
m3-l049b-matrix-of-t-in-bases.explanation: $T(v_1)=v_1$ gives the first column $(1,0)$, and $T(v_2)=0$ gives the second column $(0,0)$. In the eigenvector basis the projection is diagonal; the $1/2$ matrix is the same map in the standard basis.

m3-l049b-matrix-of-t-in-bases.prompt: Explain why a linear transformation is determined by what it does to a basis, and how to build its matrix column by column.
m3-l049b-matrix-of-t-in-bases.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) every $v=c_1v_1+\dots+c_nv_n$, so linearity gives $T(v)=c_1T(v_1)+\dots+c_nT(v_n)$ and the values $T(v_j)$ fix $T$; (2) column $j$ of the matrix holds the coordinates of $T(v_j)$ in the output basis; (3) a different choice of bases gives a different matrix for the same $T$.
m3-l049b-matrix-of-t-in-bases.modelAnswer: Any input is a combination $c_1v_1+\dots+c_nv_n$ of basis vectors, and linearity gives $T(v)=c_1T(v_1)+\dots+c_nT(v_n)$, so knowing each $T(v_j)$ determines $T$ everywhere. Write each $T(v_j)$ in the output basis; those coordinates are column $j$ of the matrix. Changing either basis changes the matrix but not the transformation.

m3-l050-composition-kernel-range.prompt: Transformation $T$ has matrix $A$ and $S$ has matrix $B$ (same basis). What is the matrix of 'apply $T$ first, then $S$'?
options: $AB$, because the first transformation is written first.
$A+B$, because transformations add.
$B^{-1}A$, because $S$ must be undone.
$BA$, since the vector meets $A$ first: $S(T(v))=B(Av)$.
m3-l050-composition-kernel-range.explanation: Composition corresponds to matrix multiplication with the later transformation on the left. That is the origin of the non-commutativity of successive rotations.

m3-l050-composition-kernel-range.prompt: What is the dimension of the kernel of $d^2/dx^2$ acting on polynomials of degree $\le4$?
m3-l050-composition-kernel-range.explanation: $p''=0$ gives $p=a+bx$, a 2-dimensional kernel. The range is the polynomials of degree $\le2$ (dimension 3); $2+3=5=\dim$ of the input space.

m3-l050-composition-kernel-range.prompt: Why is the matrix of 'apply $T$ first, then $S$' equal to $BA$ and not $AB$? Illustrate with a rotation followed by a projection.
m3-l050-composition-kernel-range.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) a vector $v$ is first multiplied by $A$ (the matrix of $T$), giving $Av$, and then by $B$, giving $B(Av)=(BA)v$; (2) the matrix written next to the vector acts first, so the order is reversed relative to the order in time; (3) the example shows the order matters: projecting then rotating differs from rotating then projecting.
m3-l050-composition-kernel-range.modelAnswer: $S(T(v))=B(Av)=(BA)v$: the matrix next to the vector acts first, so the transformation applied first appears on the right. Rotating a vector and then projecting it on the $x$-axis is not the same as projecting first and then rotating (the second keeps the vector on the $x$-axis before rotating it off), which is why $BA\ne AB$.

m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.prompt: $B=M^{-1}AM$ is similar to $A$. Which quantity is NOT necessarily the same for $A$ and $B$?
options: The eigenvalues, which are intrinsic to the transformation itself.
The eigenvectors, whose coordinate lists change with the basis.
The trace, which equals the sum of the eigenvalues in any basis.
The determinant, which is the product of the eigenvalues in any basis.
m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.explanation: Similar matrices represent the same transformation in different bases, so eigenvalues, trace and determinant (all intrinsic) agree. Eigenvectors are the same geometric directions but their coordinate lists differ: $x_B=M^{-1}x_A$.

m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.prompt: Express $v=(3,1)$ in the basis $b_1=(1,1)$, $b_2=(1,-1)$, i.e. find $c_1,c_2$ with $v=c_1b_1+c_2b_2$. Give $c_1$.
m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.explanation: Solve $c_1+c_2=3$, $c_1-c_2=1$: $c_1=2$, $c_2=1$. In general the coordinates are $M^{-1}v$ where $M$ has the basis vectors as columns.

m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(2,2)$ entry of $B=M^{-1}AM$.
m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.explanation: $AM=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, $M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ (diagonal: the columns of $M$ are the eigenvectors). The $(2,2)$ entry is $3$.

m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.prompt: Explain what a change of basis does to the coordinates of a vector and to the matrix of a transformation, and why similar matrices describe the same transformation.
m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the same vector has different coordinate lists in different bases, related by $x=Mx'$; (2) the matrix of the same transformation in the new basis is $B=M^{-1}AM$; (3) similar matrices are the same linear map written in different bases, which is why they share eigenvalues, trace and determinant.
m3-l051-change-of-basis-similar-matrices.modelAnswer: A vector keeps its identity but its coordinate list changes with the basis: $x=Mx'$ where the columns of $M$ are the new basis vectors. The same transformation then has matrix $B=M^{-1}AM$ in the new basis. Similar matrices are the same transformation seen in different coordinates, which is why their eigenvalues, trace and determinant agree.

options: Its eigenvalues are complex, so no real eigenbasis can be formed.
It is not symmetric, and only symmetric matrices can be diagonalised.
Its determinant is nonzero.
The eigenvalue 2 is repeated, yet there is only one eigenvector.
m3-l052-eigenbasis-jordan-form.explanation: $A-2I=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has a one-dimensional nullspace, so there is one eigenvector. Many nonsymmetric matrices are diagonalisable; the issue is the count of independent eigenvectors.

m3-l052-eigenbasis-jordan-form.prompt: Explain diagonalisation as 'choosing the eigenbasis', and why symmetric or Hermitian matrices always admit an orthonormal eigenbasis while a defective matrix does not admit any.
m3-l052-eigenbasis-jordan-form.rubric: Full credit requires: in the eigenbasis the transformation acts as independent stretches (diagonal matrix $\Lambda=S^{-1}AS$); spectral theorem for symmetric/Hermitian; defective = not enough eigenvectors, only a Jordan block (eigenvalue plus a nilpotent shear) is achievable.
m3-l052-eigenbasis-jordan-form.modelAnswer: If we use eigenvectors as the coordinate directions, $A$ just stretches each coordinate by its eigenvalue, so the matrix is diagonal: $\Lambda=S^{-1}AS$. Symmetric/Hermitian matrices always have a full set of mutually orthogonal eigenvectors (spectral theorem), so the basis can be chosen orthonormal. A defective matrix has a repeated eigenvalue without enough independent eigenvectors, so the best one can do is a Jordan form: the eigenvalue on the diagonal plus a 1 above it, which represents a stretch combined with a shear.

m3-l052-eigenbasis-jordan-form.prompt: The Jordan block $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ cannot be diagonalised. Compute the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^5$.
m3-l052-eigenbasis-jordan-form.explanation: For a Jordan block $J^n=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda^n&n\lambda^{n-1}\\0&\lambda^n\end{pmatrix}$, so the $(1,2)$ entry of $A^5$ is $5\cdot3^4=405$. The extra factor $n$ is the signature of a defective matrix (compare $te^{\lambda t}$ for ODEs).

m3-l053-abstract-vector-spaces-function-.prompt: With the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-1}^{1}fg\,dx$, which pair of functions is orthogonal?
options: $x$ and $x^2$, because $x^3$ is odd and its integral over $[-1,1]$ is zero.
$1$ and $x^2$, because one is constant and the other is even.
$x$ and $x$, because a function is always orthogonal to itself.
$1$ and $1$, because the constant function is the simplest vector.
m3-l053-abstract-vector-spaces-function-.explanation: $\int_{-1}^{1}x^3dx=0$. But $\int 1\cdot x^2dx=2/3\ne0$ and a nonzero function is never orthogonal to itself ($\langle f,f\rangle=\int f^2>0$). Gram-Schmidt on $1,x,x^2$ then yields Legendre polynomials.

m3-l053-abstract-vector-spaces-function-.prompt: Project $f=x^3$ onto $x$ in this function space: find $\langle x^3,x\rangle/\langle x,x\rangle$ on $[-1,1]$.
m3-l053-abstract-vector-spaces-function-.explanation: $\int x^4dx=2/5$ and $\int x^2dx=2/3$, so the coefficient is $(2/5)/(2/3)=3/5=0.6$. The remainder $x^3-\tfrac35x$ is orthogonal to $x$ (it is proportional to $P_3$).

m3-l053-abstract-vector-spaces-function-.prompt: What is the analogy between functions and vectors, and between Hermitian matrices and self-adjoint operators, that lets us treat Fourier or Legendre expansions as 'projection onto a basis'?
m3-l053-abstract-vector-spaces-function-.rubric: Full credit requires: functions as vectors in a space with inner product $\int fg$; orthogonal basis functions with coefficients = inner products ($\langle f,\phi_n\rangle/\langle\phi_n,\phi_n\rangle$); self-adjoint operator ~ Hermitian matrix with real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenfunctions, so an expansion is a change of basis.
m3-l053-abstract-vector-spaces-function-.modelAnswer: A function can be thought of as an infinite list of values, with an inner product $\int f^*g$ playing the role of the dot product. Then a set of orthogonal functions such as sines or Legendre polynomials is an orthogonal basis, and the expansion coefficient of $f$ is the projection $\langle f,\phi_n\rangle/\langle\phi_n,\phi_n\rangle$, just as with vectors. Self-adjoint differential operators play the role of Hermitian matrices, with real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenfunctions, which supplies the natural bases.

m3-l054-legendre-gram-schmidt-self-adjoi.prompt: Why are eigenfunctions of a self-adjoint (Hermitian) operator with different eigenvalues orthogonal?
options: Eigenfunctions are always chosen to be sines and cosines of the variable.
Differential operators always have orthogonal solutions, whatever their form.
Self-adjointness gives $(\lambda_1-\lambda_2)\langle f_1,f_2\rangle=0$.
Eigenvalues are defined to be orthogonal when they are distinct numbers.
m3-l054-legendre-gram-schmidt-self-adjoi.explanation: The proof is the same as for Hermitian matrices, with the inner product replaced by an integral. It is why energy eigenfunctions of different energies are orthogonal in quantum mechanics.

m3-l054-legendre-gram-schmidt-self-adjoi.prompt: Run Gram-Schmidt on $\{1,x,x^2\}$ on $[-1,1]$ with weight 1. The second orthogonal polynomial is $x^2-c$. What is $c$?
m3-l054-legendre-gram-schmidt-self-adjoi.explanation: $c=\langle x^2,1\rangle/\langle1,1\rangle=(2/3)/2=1/3$, giving $x^2-\tfrac13\propto P_2(x)$ (with $x$ already orthogonal to both by parity).

m3-l054-legendre-gram-schmidt-self-adjoi.prompt: Describe how Gram-Schmidt applied to $1,x,x^2,\dots$ on $[-1,1]$ with weight 1 produces the Legendre polynomials, and why each polynomial comes out as an even or odd function.
m3-l054-legendre-gram-schmidt-self-adjoi.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) start with $p_0=1$ and subtract from each new power its projections onto all earlier polynomials using $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-1}^1fg\,dx$; (2) e.g. $p_1=x$ and $p_2=x^2-\tfrac13$; (3) the interval and weight are symmetric under $x\to-x$, so even and odd powers are automatically orthogonal, and each $p_n$ contains only powers of the same parity as $n$.
m3-l054-legendre-gram-schmidt-self-adjoi.modelAnswer: Start with $p_0=1$, then subtract from each new power its components along the earlier polynomials using $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-1}^{1}fg\,dx$: $p_1=x$, $p_2=x^2-\tfrac13$, and so on (these are Legendre polynomials up to normalisation). The interval and weight are symmetric under $x\to-x$, so even powers are orthogonal to odd ones, and each $p_n$ contains only powers with the same parity as $n$.

m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.prompt: Two Hermitian matrices $A$ and $B$ satisfy $AB=BA$. What follows?
options: They must have exactly the same set of eigenvalues as each other.
They must be scalar multiples of one another.
They share a complete orthonormal set of eigenvectors.
Nothing can be said about their eigenvectors without more information.
m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.explanation: If $Ax=\lambda x$ then $B(Ax)=A(Bx)$ means $Bx$ is also in the eigenspace of $\lambda$, so $B$ can be diagonalised within each eigenspace. They need not have the same eigenvalues, only the same eigenvectors.

m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.prompt: The spin operators $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_z$ do not commute. What does this mean physically?
options: No state has definite values of both, and an uncertainty relation applies.
Both can be measured to any precision, but only in a fixed order.
Neither operator has eigenvalues, so neither can be measured at all.
They describe the same measurement made in two different unit systems.
m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.explanation: Commuting observables share eigenstates, so definite values for both are possible. Non-commuting ones have no common eigenbasis, which is the matrix-level origin of the uncertainty principle.

m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.prompt: Compute the commutator $[A,B]=AB-BA$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and give its $(1,2)$ entry.
m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.explanation: $AB=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $[A,B]=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$. This is $-2i\sigma_y$, consistent with $[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]=-2i\sigma_y$.

m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.prompt: Explain why commuting observables can be measured simultaneously, and how a two-spin Hilbert space is built from a Kronecker product.
m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.rubric: Full credit requires: commuting Hermitian operators share eigenvectors, so a state can have definite values of both; for two spins, basis states are $|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle$ (dimension $2\times2=4$) and an operator on spin 1 alone is $A\otimes I$, on spin 2 alone $I\otimes B$ (Kronecker products).
m3-l055-commutators-compatible-observabl.modelAnswer: If two Hermitian operators commute they can be diagonalised together, so there are states that are simultaneously eigenstates of both and a measurement of one does not disturb the other. For two spin-1/2 particles the joint state space has basis $|a\rangle\otimes|b\rangle$, dimension $4$; an operator acting only on spin 1 is $A\otimes I$ and one acting only on spin 2 is $I\otimes B$, and these commute, as operators on different spins should. A coupled-spin Hamiltonian is a sum of such Kronecker products.

m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.prompt: Which commutation relation do the Pauli matrices satisfy?
options: $[\sigma_x,\sigma_y]=0$, since all three matrices are Hermitian.
$[\sigma_x,\sigma_y]=2i\,\sigma_z$, together with its cyclic permutations.
$[\sigma_x,\sigma_y]=2\,\sigma_z$, with no factor of $i$.
$[\sigma_x,\sigma_y]=i\,\sigma_z$, the same factor as for spin operators.
m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.explanation: Multiplying out, $\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$ and $\sigma_y\sigma_x=-i\sigma_z$, so the commutator is $2i\sigma_z$. The spin operators $S=\tfrac\hbar2\sigma$ then satisfy $[S_x,S_y]=i\hbar S_z$.

m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.prompt: A molecule has 5 coupled spin-1/2 nuclei. What is the dimension of its spin Hilbert space (the Kronecker product of five $2\times2$ spaces)?
m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.explanation: Dimensions multiply: $2^5=32$. The spin Hamiltonian is a $32\times32$ Hermitian matrix built from Kronecker products, which is why simulating NMR of large spin systems grows costly.

m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.prompt: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, find the $(1,4)$ entry of the Kronecker product $A\otimes B$.
m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.explanation: $A\otimes B=\begin{pmatrix}a_{11}B&a_{12}B\\a_{21}B&a_{22}B\end{pmatrix}$. The $(1,4)$ entry lies in the top-right block $a_{12}B=2B$, in position $(1,2)$ of that block: $2\cdot1=2$.

m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.prompt: Why do two coupled spin-1/2 nuclei need a 4-dimensional Hilbert space, and how is a coupling term such as $J\,\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z$ built from single-spin operators?
m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) each spin has a 2-dimensional space and the composite system has the Kronecker product space of dimension $2\times2=4$ (basis $\uparrow\uparrow,\uparrow\downarrow,\downarrow\uparrow,\downarrow\downarrow$); (2) a single-spin operator acting on spin 1 is $A\otimes I$, and on spin 2 is $I\otimes B$; (3) a coupling is the Kronecker product of operators on both spins, $\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z$, which is diagonal in the product basis with entries $\pm1$.
m3-l056-tensor-products-pauli-algebra-co.modelAnswer: Each spin-1/2 has a two-dimensional space, and the composite system lives in the Kronecker product space of dimension $2\times2=4$, with basis $\uparrow\uparrow,\uparrow\downarrow,\downarrow\uparrow,\downarrow\downarrow$. An operator on spin 1 alone is $A\otimes I$ and on spin 2 alone $I\otimes B$; a coupling such as $J\sigma_z\otimes\sigma_z$ acts on both and is diagonal in the product basis with entries $\pm J$.
